Input: Can general relativity be considered a quantum theory? If yes, what are some examples of its application in that field? No, general relativity is not a quantum theory. It is a classical field theory, like Maxwell’s electromagnetism. Maxwell’s theory can be “quantized”, which is to say it is possible to turn it into a mathematically self-consistent quantum field theory. The biggest problem with quantization is that the resulting quantum field theory may appear nonsensical at first, producing divergent (infinite) results. However, there in many cases, these divergences are superficial in nature, and a more thorough analysis reveals that quantities that correspond to things we can actually observe consistently remain finite. These theories are said to be renormalizable. Unfortunately, for general relativity this approach does not lead to a renormalizable quantum field theory. Which is why so much effort has been made in the past several decades, trying to come up with alternative ways to tame general relativity and arrive at a self-consistent quantum theory. The biggest problem is lack of data: quantum effects of gravitation, if they exist at all, are so weak, they may forever remain undetectable. So we have competing approaches but few or no hints from Nature as to which one is worth pursuing. But no, as I said at the beginning of my answer, general relativity is a classical theory of gravitation, not a quantum theory. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can you explain the difference between "dark matter" and "dark energy"? What is the proportion of each in our universe? Certainly. It has to do with pressure. Cosmologists are simple-minded folks. They realized that on the largest of scales, the universe is rather uniform: it is more or less, on average, the same everywhere and it has no preferred direction. Which means, among other things, that its content can be modeled as an “isotropic perfect fluid”: a medium that has no shear, no viscosity, only density and pressure, and its pressure is independent of direction. But how much pressure? Well, for something this simple, there’s a rather simplistic mathematical representation: the “equation of state”, w = p / ρ . Here, p is the pressure and ρ is the energy density. (Remember, energy is just mass times speed-of-light squared, so energy density vs. mass density really are the same thing.) The beauty of this expression is that p and ρ are measured using the same units. How come, you may wonder? Well… pressure is force divided by area. Energy is force times distance; and volume is area times length (i.e., distance). So energy density would be (force times distance) divided by (area times distance), which is force divided by area… same as pressure. Therefore, the ratio w of these two is just a pure number, a “dimensionless” quantity. But what is it? Well… what if there is no pressure? That would be w = 0. Cosmologists call this “dust”. (Did I mention they’re simple-minded?) As it turns out, most ordinary matter is well approximated as “dust”. Only immensely hot matter, in which particles zip about at relativistic speeds, will have a value that substantially differs from zero. How substantially? In the extreme limit of an “ultrarelativistic gas”, w = 1 / 3. But the equations actually allow more extreme values, values outside the range between 0 and 1/3. In fact, we can have w = 1. Beyond that, w > 1 will not work as it implies a medium in which sound travels faster than the vacuum speed of light! But anything below 1 is okay. In fact, w can be negative! Yes, negative pressure. (Think about it: when particles of a gas repel each other, we have positive pressure. So if they were to attract each other, “clump”, that would be negative pressure.) As a matter of fact, any value w ≥ − 1 will do. (Stuff with w < − 1 would yield an unstable universe.) OK, one more piece to the puzzle: as the universe expands, the energy density of this stuff changes. But the energy density also involves the energy of interactions between particles of this stuff. For this reason, only the energy density of “dust” will change as the inverse of volume. In fact, at one extreme of the scale, at w = − 1 , the energy density of this stuff remains constant even as the universe expands! This is important, as you shall see in a moment. So then… our postulate is that the universe consists of such an isotropic perfect fluid, or perhaps a mix of isotropic perfect fluids. But what kind? How much? Well… we look at observation. The age of the universe. The statistical distribution of matter. Minute fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background. Distant supernovas. Long story short, we find that the universe “works” if it consists of roughly 30% “dust” and 70% of stuff with w = − 1 , together making up 100% of the so-called “critical density”, which is needed for a universe in which the geometry of space is Euclidean on average. The problem is that the actual stuff that we see: Stars, gas, dust (actual dust, not “dust”), etc., amounts to only about 4%. The remaining 96% has to be something else. We call the missing 26% of “dust” “dark matter”; and the missing 70% of stuff with w = − 1 “dark energy”. There is a lot of speculation as to what this “dark matter” and this “dark energy” are. But we don’t know. So far, experiments designed to detect these mediums directly all came up empty. We infer their existence from gravity and cosmological observations; we have not seen either. However, what we do know if our hypotheses are correct is that as the universe ages and expands, “dust” gets diluted; stuff with w = − 1 does not. So over time, “dark energy” dominates. In fact, it already does, which means that (due to its negative pressure) it is already accelerating the rate at which the universe expands. So there. That’s what dark matter and dark energy are, and this is pretty much all that we actually know about them. There’s plenty of speculation, to be sure, but speculation, even informed speculation, is not knowledge. Oh, how nice. Quora again offered some Stable Diffusion illustrations to accompany my answer. Is it possible for an object to become heavier than anything else in existence, including black holes, if it reaches lightspeed through acceleration? Objects do not become heavier by acceleration. Objects gain kinetic energy by acceleration, as measured in the reference frame of other objects that do not accelerate along with the object in question. Decades ago, relativity texts often introduced the concept of “relativistic mass”, which lumped together the (intrinsic) rest mass of the moving object with its (observer-dependent) kinetic energy. Fortunately, this concept is not much used anymore and, well, good riddance, because it led to a lot of misunderstandings. So no, an object will not become heavier no matter how close to the vacuum speed of light it moves in some observer’s reference frame. (Keep in mind that motion is always relative: objects move relative to other objects, in their own reference frames they are always at rest.) If a light ray of white light is bent by the gravity of a massive object like a star, does the light ray undergo diffraction and turn into a rainbow? No, it does not, and that is a very important point. The refractive index of transparent materials tends to depend on wavelength. That is to say, light rays of different color will travel at different speeds in that material, and therefore follow different paths. This is why a lens, a prism can split a white ray of light into its constituent colors, creating a rainbow pattern. Gravitational lensing is different, and this has to do fundamentally with the weak equivalence principle. Gravitation is an “equal opportunity” interaction: It does not care about the material properties of the thing that is affected by it. Two rays of light following identical trajectories will be deflected by an identical amount, regardless of their color. This would not be the case, mind you, if the speed of light itself depended on wavelength. And that would be the case if light was a result of an interaction mediated by a particle with mass. But electromagnetism, the interaction behind light, is not mediated by a massive particle. It is mediated by photons, which are massless, so always travel at the vacuum speed of light regardless of their kinetic energy (which in turn determines their frequency, i.e., their color.) So red light and blue light, for instance, despite being substantially different in terms of the energy of the individual photons, will follow the same path in a gravitational field. Having said all that, it is still possible for a gravitational field to produce a rainbow-like effect, but for a different reason. Here is an example of a simulated projection by a gravitational lens with that is not perfectly spherical (i.e., it has a quadrupole mass moment), of light from a point source onto a projection surface: The reason why the colors of the rainbow appear in this image is not because the gravitational lens affected light of different color differently. Rather, it has to do with the constructive/destructive interference of the light wavefront as it arrives at the projection surface; the peaks and valleys of this interference pattern are wavelength-dependent, so we see, e.g., red peaks vs. blue peaks at different locations. In quantum mechanics, is there any context where an electron has a definite position and velocity simultaneously? If such a context exists, are there known real-world situations where this is observed, or is it purely theoretical? No. A “definite” position or momentum (let’s be pedantic here and use momentum in lieu of velocity) means that both position and momentum are number-valued. That is to say, the particle is simultaneously in a “position eigenstate” and a “momentum eigenstate”. Let me explain what that means. In quantum mechanics, positions ^ q and momenta ^ p are not representable by numbers (hence the little “hat” over the symbols). They can be represented using a form of matrix algebra, or they can be represented using function operators. The fundamental statement of quantum physics is that these two things do not commute under multiplication: ^ p ^ q − ^ q ^ p = − i ℏ , where i is the imaginary unit and ℏ is the reduced Planck constant. Pretty much everything else in quantum physics follows from this commutation relation, including the famed uncertainty principle. Whether we express positions and momenta using matrices or operators, these things act upon the state of the system (which may be represented by the famous wavefunction). In the Copenhagen interpretation, we interpret this wavefunction as a probability amplitude, and use it to estimate the probability of a future experiment based on measurement results available to us at present. But measurement results are numbers, whereas ^ p and ^ q are not. Except when they are being measured! An act of measurement confines either ^ p or ^ q to an “eigenstate”, which is to say that when it acts of the wavefunction, it’s action is like multiplying the wavefunction by a number. This number is our measurement result. Now suppose that we somehow find a trick and simultaneously measure ^ p and ^ q so they are both numbers. But numbers commute under multiplication! The quantity p q − q p = 0 is always zero (notice that I dropped the hats, as p and q are supposed to be ordinary numbers now). This violates the fundamental canonical commutation relation. So either quantum mechanics is wrong, or this cannot happen: ^ p and ^ q cannot simultaneously be numbers. We know from countless experiments that quantum mechanics is not wrong, however weird it can be. Therefore, we are left with the conclusion that no, a particle cannot simultaneously be in a position and a momentum eigenstate. This was of course just a very superficial sketch of the math behind quantum physics, and, yes, it’s counterintuitive. As I stressed many times, do not expect to intuit the quantum world. It does not work that way. It’s one of those rare instances where intuition not only does not help you, it might become a formidable obstacle. Like it or not, to make sense of the quantum world, math is essential, as math is the only language that we have by which this world can be made sense of. If there is a very, very tall tower, and a light source that spins around the top of it at a very high speed, would the shadow it casts ever be able to move faster than the speed of light? Indeed, shadows, spots of light, even the start of the gap in a ginormous pair of scissors can move faster than the vacuum speed of light. So in theory, with a large enough laser pointer moving fast enough, you could create a spot of light on the surface of the Moon that moves around at a speed many times greater than the vacuum speed of light. Shadows can do this, too; in fact, when we infer, for instance, the existence of a planet orbiting another star when it briefly transits in front of that star, the shadow of that planet traverses our solar system typically much faster than the vacuum speed of light, as it crosses the Earth’s orbit. There is one common theme in these examples. None of them can carry energy-momentum or information from point A to point B. You can make a laser spot traverse the Moon very fast, but two astronauts standing on the lunar surface will not be able to manipulate that spot and use it to send messages to one another. There is another thing that can travel faster than the vacuum speed of light: light! That is to say, the so-called phase velocity of light. In some ionized mediums with an index of refraction less than one, the phase velocity is greater than c . But again, the phase velocity is not something that can be used to carry a useful signal. Is it really true when the action lab said that if negative mass exists, it would chase a positive mass and the positive mass would repel accelerating until it sped up faster than the speed of light? First of all, negative mass almost certainly does not exist in this universe. Be thankful that it doesn’t: If it did, its mass-energy content being less than zero, it would allow the vacuum to decay into negative mass particles, implying that our entire universe is unstable, subject to collapse. Not exactly a desirable prospect. Having said that, if negative mass did exist, then, at least in the context of classical (be it relativistic or nonrelativistic) gravitational theory, it would indeed repeal everything; however, it would still be attracted to positive masses. The result would be as you describe: If we had, say, a device with a negative and a positive mass of equal magnitude, the positive mass would be pushed by the negative mass, but the negative mass would be pulled by the positive mass, so there would be an unceasing net acceleration. And no, it would not violate conservation laws either, since the total mass of this particular system would be zero, hence its kinetic energy and momentum would also be zero. But no, not even this system would speed up beyond the vacuum speed of light. As viewed by a distant observer, its acceleration would bring it ever closer to the vacuum speed of light but never quite reaching it. It would behave just like the classic Internet physics FAQ example of the relativistic rocket under constant acceleration. Long story short, negative mass may have the power to destroy our universe through eternal quantum collapse, but it still does not have the power to alter the basic principles of relativity theory. If black holes' horizons form infinitely far in the future, then how can they evaporate in finite time? You stumbled upon a key potential contradiction between two things: But first: it is not the horizon that evaporates. Indeed, contrary to popular explanations (including Hawking’s own, from his popular science book) the actual equations tell a different story: Hawking radiation exists because the black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse and therefore, the past and the future boundary conditions are not identical. It is this difference that manifests itself in what distant observers see as outgoing radiation. (As an important aside, it should be mentioned that the characteristic wavelength of Hawking radiation is around 20 times the Schwarzschild radius. That alone should inform us that the horizon is not the source of that radiation.) So what does this mean? Do horizons never form? Maybe. Does a collapsing, evaporating black hole leave behind a “naked singularity”? Maybe. Does something else happen? Who knows, as the final moments of a black hole’s existence take place at the Planck scale, and we know nothing about the Planck scale, especially nothing about how gravity behaves at the Planck scale. The one thing we do know is that Hawking radiation is not predicated on the present-day existence of a horizon. If it were, there would be no Hawking radiation in the first place, since the horizon, even in classical general relativity, remains forever in any outside observer’s future.

What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++? The propagator for a massless scalar field, which obeys the Klein-Gordon equation ∂ μ ∂ μ ϕ = 0 , can be derived from the Green’s function of this equation, ∂ μ ∂ μ G ( x − y ) = δ 4 ( x − y ) that, in momentum space, becomes − k 2 ~ G ( k ) = − 1 , hence ~ G ( k ) = 1 k 2 + i ϵ , where we introduced a small imaginary term, as usual, to avoid the singularity at k = 0. By itself, this expression is not something you would compute numerically in a language such as C++. You may be able to derive expressions of this sort in computer algebra (either general purpose CAS with specialized packages or special purpose systems). The propagator is used in combination with the vertex rules of a theory to compute cross-sections corresponding to particle interactions. That computation itself may not be trivial as it involves divergent integrals that may need to be regularized in order to obtain meaningful results for observable quantities. In short, no, unless you first use C++ to build a CAS for quantum field theory, you would not be using C++ for this type of computation. You might use a CAS to derive an expression for an observable quantity that you then import into a C++ program for numerical evaluation (perhaps as part of a larger computation) but the propagator on its own is not something you’d likely use in C++. Near Earth, in the Newtonian limit, gravity is 99.9999% due to warping of time (the “gravitational time dilation”) and only about 0.0001% due to the warping of space. How do you calculate these values? The actual calculation gets a little bit involved, as it requires writing down the equations of motion (geodesic equations) of a particle in the Schwarzschild metric (characterizing the gravitational field of a spherically symmetric body outside of that body) and then using a suitable approximation, such as the post-Newtonian approximation, to find approximate solutions. However, the result, especially for a particle initially at rest, is fairly simple. Its initial radial acceleration in the gravitational field of a mass M is given by a = − G M r 2 ( 1 − 2 ( β + γ ) G M c 2 r ) . The first part of the expression on the right-hand side is just the Newtonian acceleration (inverse square law). It is, however, multiplied by the term in parenthesis, which contains contributions both due to the nonlinearity of gravity, characterized by β , and the spatial curvature, characterized by γ . For general relativity, β = γ = 1 , but these so-called Eddington-parameters can also accommodate alternative theories of gravitation. When you calculate the magnitude of the correction, it comes to about 2.8 parts in a billion, give or take, here on the surface of the Earth. Once the particle is in motion, the post-Newtonian equation of motion becomes more complicated, but this simple expression should give you an idea as to the magnitude and nature of the correction. (See also https://descanso.jpl.nasa.gov/monograph/series2/Descanso2_all.pdf where these so-called post-Newtonian equations of motion are discussed in detail and put to practical use.) Why were the breakthroughs in the development of physics from 1900 to 1935 far greater than subsequent period? It seems that those 35 years were the period of the greatest explosion in the development of physics in the entire science history. Is the premise of this question really valid? Permit me to challenge it. Certainly, the first one third of the 20th century saw not one but two extraordinary revolutions in physics, the development of relativity theory and that of the quantum theory. But similar, profound revolutions have taken place previously. Perhaps the biggest, I’d argue, something even more profound than the development of quantum physics and relativity, was the shift from the Aristotelian to the modern view of the physical world. In Aristotle’s view, the celestial spheres and the terrestrial sphere were governed by different laws. In the celestial spheres, motion was eternal. In the terrestrial sphere, motion was temporary, always coming to an end without a mover of some sort. The celestial spheres were “perfect”, unchanging, whereas the terrestrial sphere was subject to decay. With the work of Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo, and ultimately, Newton, this was replaced by a world view in which the same fundamental laws governed heaven and earth. And these fundamental laws became precise, expressed using the language of mathematics, in particular the mathematics of infinitesimal changes, i.e., calculus. I cannot stress how fundamental this shift was to the development of modern science. Compared to this, the birth of quantum physics and the theory of relativity are… well, almost child’s play. Moving on, in the late 18th and the 19th century, another groundbreaking development took place: the advent of the “action principle”, the idea that the equations that govern a physical system can be derived by minimizing the “action”, a mathematical expression that characterizes a system’s evolution over time. It is difficult to stress just how critical the action principle has become in nearly all branches of fundamental physics: It governs mechanical systems, both particles and continua; classical field theories (electromagnetism and gravitation); and it forms an absolutely crucial foundation for the quantum theory. And no, physics did not come to an end in the 1930s. What was yet to happen was the development of quantum field theory, including non-Abelian theories, the modern understanding of the role intrinsic symmetries play in the behavior of quantum fields, ultimately leading to the development of the Standard Model of particle physics, a model that (as far as we know) accurately describes all the fundamental building blocks of the universe excluding gravitation. So yes, the first third of the 20th century was a remarkable period in physics, when two major revolutions took place at the same time. But that does not mean that similar, profound shifts in our understanding have not taken place before or after. And not just in physics; how about, for instance, biology, the understanding of DNA and the molecular foundations of genetics, that took place in the 1950s? It is perhaps true that fundamental physics has been a bit “stuck” in the past 50 years, not so much for lack of ideas but for lack of experimental evidence: Without hints from Nature, we can’t tell which approach, e.g., makes better sense as we try to improve the compatibility of the quantum theory and gravitation. Even so, look at the application side of things. It wasn’t that long ago that things like a blue LED seemed like unachievable “holy grails” in semiconductor technology, yet here we are, chances are you are reading this on a device with an OLED display, sitting in a room lit by a high power white LED lightbulb. Or not. Maybe you are not reading my silly words at all, consulting instead with a large language model, a culmination of some 70 years of research that began with simple “neural networks” designed to simulate the basic structure of neurons in the animal brain? So breakthroughs happen all the time. The first 30-odd years of the 20th century must have been an amazing time to be alive for a physicist, but you know what, I much rather do physics in 2024, with all the knowledge we have since added in the intervening century. Is it possible that centrifugal force is caused by a curvature of spacetime? In the context of general relativity, the gravitational force and the centrifugal force have many similarities. Basically, both forces can be viewed as “pseudoforces” that arise in non-inertial reference frames. And both can be accounted for using the same mathematical machinery of covariant derivatives, Christoffel-symbols and the whole kaboodle. However, there is a crucial difference. In the case of the centrifugal force, spacetime curvature is zero. The pseudoforce arises because we are measuring it in a noninertial (rotating) reference frame. In contrast, in the case of gravity, spacetime curvature is not zero. There is no global coordinate transformation that can remove the effects of gravitation. Locally it is always possible to define inertial (freely falling) reference frames, but there is no “global family of inertial observers” who are at rest, or moving at uniform velocity, relative to each other. Another way of looking at it is this: There is a crucial distinction between the use of a curvilinear coordinate system (such as the coordinate system of a rotating reference frame) in flat spacetime, vs. curved spacetime, even though the mathematical tools that we can use to investigate them are the same.

Since we cannot observe an object crossing an event horizon, does this mean we cannot ever observe an object expanding out of the observable universe? Will it just get more and more redshifted forever? Meaning there is no “un observable” universe? Yes, to the first part of the question. If you were to watch a distant galaxy, you would never see it cross your cosmological event horizon. Its light would simply become more and more redshifted. But no, that does not mean that there is no “un observable” universe. It simply implies that there are parts of the universe that almost certainly exist, but which we cannot ever observe. And that’s why I added the “almost certainly” qualifier. For all I know, just beyond the limits of the observable universe, everything changes, it’s all dancing pink unicorns in whipped cream or something equally silly. If that is the case, we would never know. However, if we assume that by and large, the same rules govern the universe everywhere, including beyond the limits of its observable bits, then pink unicorns are out, and in all likelihood, the universe is still its same old boring self, mostly empty, with galaxies and stars and planets floating around in the void, even far beyond the boundaries of the observable universe. What we call gravitational acceleration (9.8ms2) is a phenomenon observable only by the observer on the ground due to the dilation of time, which passes more slowly for him, giving the impression that the object in free fall is accelerating? No, that is not the way it works. At the Newtonian level, gravitational acceleration is simply a result of a force, acting at a distance between any two objects. If one of the objects is the Earth and the other is, well, anything at or near the surface of the Earth, that object will accelerate towards the center of the Earth at approximately 9.8 meters per seconds squared. In general relativity, the corresponding Newtonian potential is ascribed to the spacetime metric, specifically the “time” part of the metric that determines the rate at which clocks tick. And indeed, in a gravitational field, clocks tick more slowly than far away from the gravitating object. But this difference is minuscule. It’s barely more than one part in a billion. Tiny, tiny, tiny. So no, gravitational acceleration is not some illusion that we see because of gravitational time dilation. It is a very real deviation from straight-line, constant velocity motion. How real? Well, drop something not too heavy (we don’t want any injuries here) on your foot to find out! However, the reason why this deviation exists, why objects accelerate toward each other, is much more subtle. When we write down the relativistic equations of motion, they represent trajectories in “spacetime”. Don’t let this phrase mislead you. It’s nothing mysterious. If you draw a simple plot, with, say, time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical, and use it to characterize the motion of something, you drew a plot in spacetime. The thing is, the path connecting an initial state and a final state for any trajectory will have certain geometric properties in general relativity. This causes the path to be “bent”, representing a trajectory with changing velocity, i.e., acceleration. Ultimately, this bending occurs because the “length” of a trajectory is not measured in the conventional way, but in a way prescribed by the theory (Riemannian geometry, actually). The actual calculation is not terribly difficult but it cannot be explained easily as there are mathematical prerequisites for the formulas to make sense (the concept of geodesics, connection coefficients, covariant derivatives, etc.) Long story short, time dilation is minuscule (around one part in a billion) but it’s enough to change trajectories to produce a very real (not illusionary) downward acceleration (9.8 meters per seconds squared here on the surface of the Earth) by altering the trajectories of free objects. Why are black holes called black holes if they are actually white or lighter than the space around them? They are neither white nor lighter than the space around them. In classical general relativity, a black hole is truly black: it absorbs all light that hits it, and emits absolutely nothing. You really cannot get more black than that. Even with Hawking radiation, the situation is similar. Sure, black holes radiate. But astrophysical black holes have Hawking temperatures that are just a tiny, tiny fraction of the temperature of the cosmic microwave background radiation. In other words, even in this case, the black hole is a lot more black than the cosmos: it absorbs many orders of magnitude more radiation than it emits. So that’s why they are called black. Again, you really cannot get more black than these things. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

In relativity won't the electromagnetic force also cause time dilation in a similar manner to gravity, considering that time dilation due to gravity arises because it causes objects to accelerate and that applies to the electromagnetic force as well? Gravitational time dilation is not due to acceleration. Gravitational time dilation is a direct effect of the gravitational field. But allow me to take a step back. In many of my answers I cautioned against taking the “geometric interpretation” of gravitation too literally. This advice is not mine; none other than Einstein himself argued against reading too much into this interpretation, and in his own published works, never ceased to refer to gravitation as a force. Yes, gravitation can be interpreted as a change in geometry. Moreover, because gravitation is universal, it affects everything the same way, regardless of material composition or other properties, and that includes our instruments with which we measure space and time. Literally, the geometry imposed by gravitation is the only geometry in town, the one-and-only geometry that we see using our instruments. Can electromagnetism be interpreted using the language of geometry? You betcha. There have been numerous classical attempts (five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein theory, Weyl’s theory of linear vs. quadratic ground-forms, Einstein’s attempt to study nonsymmetric gravitation) but also in the modern quantum fiel theory formulation, the electromagnetic interaction is represented by a so-called covariant derivative, which has a direct geometric interpretation. However! That geometry is not universal. It depends on the material properties of whatever it is that the field is acting upon. Notably, it depends on the charge-to-mass ratio. So sure, if we were to build a clock using electrically charged components and placed that clock in an electromagnetic field, its operation would change. But another clock, made from electrically neutral components, would not be sensitive to that electromagnetic field. This is not how gravity works: The presence of gravitation has the same effect on both clocks. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can I buy a quantum computer? Are they real, or are they just news wanting views? Well, yes… but no. Allow me to explain. Or rather, allow me to begin my answer with a question: What do we call a “quantum computer”? Because the definitions, unfortunately, shift depending on who is offering the announcement of the day about yet another breakthrough, yet another declaration of “quantum supremacy”, or let’s face it, yet another request for research grants. So if money is no object, what can you buy that others might call a “quantum computer”? Well, you can certainly buy an experimental device that has a couple of qubits (the basic unit characterizing the capabilities of a quantum computer). You may get one for a few thousand dollars. Not very useful or practical, mind you, just an educational toy. If you have a lot more money, you can also buy a system (or more likely, have one custom-built for you) with more qubits, but apart from the sticker shock, be prepared for the need to set up a special facility to host, and support, the hardware. And in the end it, too, would amount to little more than an expensive educational toy, with no practical utility whatsoever. Or you can buy a system like D-wave’s quantum annealer, which is basically an analog computer that is particularly suitable for certain classes of optimization problems. But it is not a general purpose quantum computer. Which leads me to the answer I’d like to offer to my own question: a true, general purpose quantum computer is a scalable quantum computing machine. One that has as many qubits as I need, one that can be expanded with more qubits if necessary. This is not something that you can buy no matter how much dough you have, because it is not something that exists today, and may never exist in the future. Some compare the current state of quantum computing to the dawn of digital computers. But that is a false comparison. Sure, the Intel 4004 CPU was very primitive compared to its present-day counterparts. But the architecture was scalable. I could, in principle, build a circuit with a thousand 4004 CPUs. I could use bank switching and attach gigabytes of memory to a single 4004 CPU. Sure it would be damn inconvenient, cumbersome and very costly, but the system would work. There is no underlying physics principle that prohibits the existence of a million-CPU supercomputer with a terabyte of RAM, based on the 4004. It would be a darn stupid thing to build, but it can exist. This is not the case with quantum computing. You cannot add qubits galore, no matter how much money you have. The culprit is fundamental physics: the famous threshold theorem, in particular. The promise of general-purpose quantum computing is based on this theorem. You see, quantum computers are based on the premise that even though qubits have only two states when they are read, during the operation of the quantum computer it’s not those two states but their superposition, characterized by a continuous quantity (e.g., the phase of the wavefunction), that interacts with similar qubits in the system. The problem is that the qubits are not only entangled with each other, they also tend to get entangled with everything else in the universe. We try to keep the qubits as isolated from the environment as possible, to prevent environmental decoherence. This isolation is necessarily imperfect. But here is where the threshold theorem kicks in: If we can keep this decoherence below a certain threshold, there exist error correction algorithms that allow a system of qubits to emulate a perfect quantum computer with fewer qubits. The trouble is, this threshold has so far proven elusive. All those machines that I mentioned above, including cheaper commercially available units or pricier research installations? None of them are scalable. None of them beat the threshold theorem. Can the theorem be beaten? An entire industry, billions of dollars are wagered on that possibility. I am in a skeptical minority: I think it will prove to be a no-go theorem. Of course it is very possible that I am wrong. But until I see a credible announcement of a quantum computer architecture that beats the threshold theorem, my skepticism remains. So then, the answer to your question is that, well, yes, you can buy systems that are called “quantum computers” and they are not deceptive, you just need to know exactly what it is that they are selling. But no, you cannot buy a true, scalable general-purpose quantum computer because no such thing exists today.

Is it a coincidence that all particles with Higgs mass carry electric charges? Not sure if I’d call it a coincidence, nor is it, strictly speaking, true. Yes, the Higgs mechanism is responsible for the rest masses of all charged fermions (charged leptons and quarks). Why not neutrinos? Well, neutrinos need a different mechanism that yields the so-called mass mixing matrix, which is the secret behind the observed neutrino flavor oscillations. The Higgs mechanism is also responsible (albeit in a different way) for the masses of the electroweak vector bosons, but here, we have both the charged W-bosons and the neutral Z-boson. So there, there’s a particle that is massive thanks to the Higgs but has no electric charge. So perhaps a pertinent question is not so much why the Higgs prefers charged particles (since most elementary particles are charged) but why neutrinos have such weird behavior when it comes to mass. What, if anything, is special about a 3 + 1 dimensional space time that makes it ideal for describing something like physics? Well, we use 3+1 dimensional spacetime to describe physics, because physics is the science of stuff in our universe, and our universe appears to be 3+1 dimensional (excluding theories like Kaluza-Klein, string theory, or other offshoots in which additional dimensions exist.) But what makes 3+1 dimensions really special? Curiously, I think there is a reason. Let’s start with space. One-dimensional space is rather boring; it’s just the number line. No structures there. Two dimensional space: that’s the plane. It is possible to create reasonably complicated things in two dimensions, but there are severe limits. All it takes is to have three houses and three utilities: you just cannot hook up all three houses to the three utilities without intersecting connections. Ouch! Oh, and forget animals with an internal pass-through digestion system. You create an animal with a passage from its mouth to… you know, the other end, and in a two-dimensional world, the poor creature falls apart into two disconnected parts. So we pretty much need three dimensions as our playground. In three dimensions, we can connect complex graphs, have complex creatures with multiple networks of piping inside their bodies, we can even tie knots that can hold things securely. So why not four spatial dimensions, then? Surely that’s better? Well… maybe not. Remember knots? They don’t exist in four dimensions. You can always lift the string out in the fourth direction and eliminate the knot without untying it. Pipes won’t hold their content either. So maybe, just maybe, four spatial dimensions is too much of a good thing. We are stuck with three. OK, how about time? Well, obviously we need at least one time dimension in order for there to be change. But what if we had two time dimensions? Not exactly a good thing. Why? Because a world with two (or more) time dimensions will be acausal. Effects may precede causes and all that. So that really settles it: we are stuck with 3+1 dimensions if we want a causal universe that has enough spatial dimensions for complexity, but not too many spatial dimensions that would destroy complexity. Is it possible to use telescopes to observe the event horizon and beyond of a black hole, or does the gravity of the black hole absorb all light before it reaches us? Here is the thing about black holes: No photon ever leaves the event horizon. This would be true even if we had pre-formed, “primordial” black holes in this universe, with fully formed event horizons. This is the very nature of an event horizon, nothing, not even light, can ever come from one. Add to this the fact that an actual, astrophysical black hole that forms as a result of gravitational collapse never really completes the process. Its event horizon remains forever in the future of any observer outside. So to “see” its event horizon, you’d need not a telescope but first and foremost, a time machine, to bring a signal from the future to the present! In short, no. Not even with an all-powerful telescope can you see what’s not actually there, namely light leaving a black hole’s event horizon. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What is beyond the event horizon of a black hole? What is on the other side of an event horizon? Think of the event horizon not so much as a place as a moment in time. For instance, if we had a cloud of dust (pressureless medium) collapsing under its own self-gravity, the “event horizon” is the moment in time when the collapse becomes irreversible. It so happens that this moment in time, for us outside the collapsing dust cloud, is forever in the future. It is a moment that literally never comes. If the dust particles were equipped with a mind of their own and had rocket engines, they could change their mind at the last split second, as close to this last moment as possible. From the particles’ perspective, we may be talking milliseconds or less For us on the outside, however, these milliseconds may mean millions of years. Or trillions. Or septillions. Really boundless: No matter how far into the future we go, there’s still a chance that the dust particles turn around and never form an event horizon in the first place. But suppose they do. The “other side”, beyond this moment in time, exists only for the dust particles. It is not something we can see from the outside. But if one of those “particles” happens to be an observer, that observer would find himself in a collapsing mini-universe. The opposite of a Big Bang scenario: a universe that ends up very hot and very dense. General relativity tells us that this may end in a “singularity”, a moment in time when the rules of physics break down, but more likely, this simply means that eventually the density and temperature reach a domain in which classical general relativity is no longer adequate, and we do not have a good quantum theory of gravitation that we can trust. But that’s the “other side”: a mini-universe that’s collapsing, ultimately crushing everyone and everything therein as it becomes extremely hot and extremely dense. Why is graviton difficult to detect? Do we have any good reasons to believe it exits in the first place? The graviton is difficult to detect because gravity is very weak, which means that the probability of any particular graviton to interact with matter is very, very, very low. The late Freeman Dyson in his 2012 Poincaré Prize lecture calculated that the Sun, in addition to the humongous amount of thermal energy it emits as electromagnetic radiation (mostly light), also emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation. Now 79 megawatts is not a lot for a star, but it is certainly a respectable amount: For comparison, we’ve been able to reliably detect a mere 8 watts in the form of a radio signal from the Pioneer 10 spacecraft when it was roughly 80 times farther from the Earth than the Sun. So Dyson calculated what it would take to detect a single graviton event, i.e., an atomic transition caused by a captured graviton, from this radiation, using the entire Earth as a perfect graviton detector. His result: We’d see roughly one graviton every billion years. That is how weakly gravity interacts with matter. Concerning the second half of the question, no, we do not “believe” that gravitons exist. Belief is done in other places. Rather, we know that if the gravitational field is a quantum field much like electromagnetism, in the so-called perturbative limit (basically, when the field is weak) it would manifest itself in the form of discrete quanta, which we call gravitons. So detecting gravitons would confirm our suspicion that gravitation, too, is a quantum phenomenon. Conversely, if we had a firm prediction that gravitons should be detected in a given experiment, and we failed to see those gravitons, that would at the very least falsify the idea that gravity is similar a a quantum field theory to electromagnetism. (Perhaps it is still a quantum theory, but something manifestly different.) The trouble is, we can do neither. We can neither detect gravitons nor reliably exclude their existence based on observations that we can do. So we end up speculating. There are plenty of theories out there, both quantum theories of gravitation and alternatives. Some are better than others, but we really have no way to decide which is right: without experiment, without observation, we are blind, and although we are reasonably clever monkeys, at no time in the history of science were we able to figure out something like this on our own, without hints from Nature as far as I know. Is a white hole short-lived if it continues to drain its energy and matter? White holes are not short-lived. In our actual universe, in all likelihood they are not long-lived either, on account of the fact that they do not exist. They are mathematical constructs, not physics. White holes represent a family of solutions of Einstein’s field equations that are “time-reversed” versions of black holes. Literally. That’s it. Replace t with − t . These are valid solutions of Einstein’s field equations. That does not mean they exist as physical reality. We (think we) know how black holes form. The seminal paper on this subject, Oppenheimer-Snyder (Phys. Rev., 1939) shows that a collapsing cloud of matter, as viewed from the outside, will appear to continue the process of collapse indefinitely, seen increasingly in slow motion by outside observers. Since then, we have figured out that the “asymptotic end state” of this collapse at future infinity is the Kerr solution (unless the cloud has electric charge) of an axisymmetric black hole. Things that fall into a black hole do not come out. Things can fall into a black hole because they were outside the black hole in the past. Time-reverse all of the above and you end up with an “asymptotic start state” that is like the Kerr solution. Its gravity is still attractive. (Imagine playing the Solar System backwards; planets are still orbiting the Sun, just going backwards. Gravity did not turn repulsive.) Yet things do not fall into it. Why? Because they are not in it in the future. Yes, that’s what time-reversal means! We flipped the law of causality: Instead of the past determining the future, it’s now the future that’s determining the past and the present. The lifetime of white holes is infinite starting from the “asymptotic starting state” but if there were such things as astrophysical white holes, their days would be numbered. Just as a black hole may be, say, 1 billion years old, a corresponding white hole would “decollapse” completely in a billion years. As it does so, it would of course continue to violate not just the principle of causality but also the second law of thermodynamics. Anyhow, if there is one thing you want to remember about white holes: they are time-reversed black holes. They are not actual astrophysical objects, they are not black holes at the end of their lives evaporating by way of Hawking radiation. They are black holes with the clock running backwards. Do electromagnetic waves have momentum? If so, do waves and sound waves have momentum? Yes, electromagnetic waves have both energy and momentum. When an object emits some light in a specific direction, it is pushed backwards ever so slightly. Similarly, when an object absorbs or reflects light, it is pushed by that light. (Experimental spacecraft with solar sails use the momentum of sunlight to accelerate.) As to sound waves, you can even visualize it. A sound wave is a pressure wave. Recall what happens when a very loud sound wave hits, say, a window pane. The glass shatters. It shatters because of the force (change in momentum) as momentum from the incoming sound wave is transferred to the glass. So yes, sound waves also carry momentum. As do waves in general. What scientific questions need to be answered in order to tackle the understanding of dark matter? Very simple: Direct detection. The existence of dark matter is widely assumed, as we observe gravitational behavior that cannot be explained otherwise within the context of general relativity: the same general relativity that, on other scales (e.g., within the solar system) works with spectacular precision. Now of course just because something works on a size scale measured by light-hours at most does not mean that it will necessarily work equally well on a size scale measured in the thousands or tens of thousands of light-years or more. Which means that there may not be dark matter at all: perhaps the laws of gravitation must be modified! But that proves to be an immensely tricky thing to do, because most modifications run into other observational constraints. Gravitational radiation, arrival times of gravitational and non-gravitational signals from the same event, cosmological observations… the bar is set very high for such modified theories of gravity. But until we have direct confirmation of dark matter, we won’t know for sure. And so far, all we have are null results: None of the attempts to search for dark matter by nongravitational means proved successful. So the jury is still out. While Hawking radiation one particle of a pair disappears in a black hole and the other one drives away from it. But why can't both of them vanish in the black hole? As pointed out in another answer, that popular explanation of Hawking radiation, despite the fact that it comes from Hawking’s own popular book, is utter rubbish. When we look at Hawking’s own 1974 paper that describes what we now call Hawking radiation, a very different picture emerges. The black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse. This is important because it presents an asymmetry between past and future. The gravitational field of the black hole is responsible for what is known as gravitational vacuum polarization (rather crudely, conditions change as we approach the black hole, so the vacuum is “not the same” at different distances from it). When we apply quantum field theory, the differences between the past and the future, when applied as boundary conditions to describe the effects of vacuum polarization, result in a net outflow of radiation. The wavelength of this radiation is a bit of a giveaway already. The peak wavelength is roughly 20 times the black hole’s Schwarzschild radius. That alone ought to tell us that we’re not producing teeny-weeny particles near the event horizon; rather, the entire vicinity of the object is a source of radiation, due to the extreme effects of gravity. Or maybe not so extreme. The same equations can be applied to any system, really. Gravitational vacuum polarization is present wherever gravity is present. The difference is that a black hole is very, very compact so we can get very close to it and still stay in space. Just take the Earth: You cannot get any closer to its center than about 6,370 kilometers before hitting its surface. Replace the Earth with a black hole of the same mass and it’s less than a centimeter in size! When we get that close, there are of course more pronounced gravitational effects than at a distance of thousands of kilometers from the center. Of course “more pronounced” is in the eye of the beholder: an Earth-mass black hole would still only produce about 10 − 17 watts of radiative power, mostly in the microwave band. (This value, curiously, is about the same as the received signal strength from some of our most distant spacecraft, as picked up by the very large antennas of NASA’s deep space network.) Is Sagittarius A star, the supermassive black hole in the center of the Milky Way actually in the center? Sgr A* is in the “central region” of the Milky Way. The role this supermassive black hole may or may not have played in the formation of the Milky Way remains ill understood. However, there really is no such thing as “the center”. The center of what? The Milky Way? Which things are part of the Milky Way? What about distant star clusters orbiting the Milky Way? Satellite galaxies? Eventually it becomes a matter of convention. However we define the Milky Way, there corresponds to it a center-of-mass. But a different definition places that center-of-mass at a different location. Something similar happens here in the solar system. Astronomers, folks navigating spacecraft often talk about the SSB, the solar system barycenter. Sounds great until you ask… exactly what is used to calculate its location? Suppose we discover an ice giant, a Jupiter-sized planet somewhere in the Kuiper belt. A mass that large, that far from the Sun, if it is considered part of the solar system, would dramatically shift the defined location of the SSB. One definition is no more valid than another; it’s a matter of convention, not physics. What is physics is that in the solar system, the mass of the Sun dominates. Everything else is just debris. Planets do not orbit the SSB (yes, I know, even some NASA Web pages say that they do; those pages are plain wrong.) They follow elliptical orbits with the planet+Sun two body system’s center-of-mass as its focal point, with gravitation from the other planets only contributing minor perturbations. So the Earth orbits the Sun-Earth two-body system barycenter, with slight perturbations from Jupiter and the other planets; this barycenter is distinct from the Sun-Jupiter barycenter that Jupiter orbits. Going back to Sgr A*, it does not play a similar, dominating role in the Milky Way. It is massive, but its mass is dwarfed by… Never mind the whole Milky Way, the central region itself has thousands of times the mass of Sgr A*. So other stars in the Milky Way, including our own Sun, do not orbit Sgr A*. In a crude approximation, they orbit the barycenter of the central bulge of the Milky Way. That includes Sgr A* of course, but it is not dominated by it, not even close. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why is light a particle and a wave at the same time? Can you explain the two slot experiment? “Wave-particle duality” is another one of those unfortunate phrases that are invented to help explain a difficult concept, but do more harm than good in the end. So here is the thing when it comes to quantum phenomena: the exact outcome of a measurement, carried out using a classical instrument (say, the human eyeball) cannot be predicted. We can only predict probabilities. But it’s not like “classical” probabilities. The limitation does not arise from the fact that we lack full knowledge of the system. Rather, the exact outcome of an experiment does not exist until, well, until it exists. It is not some technological limitation: it is not predictable in principle. But then… what can we predict? We can predict probabilities. And these probabilities are governed by an equation that, for all practical intents and purposes, travel like a wave. Waves that interfere with one another. Waves that reinforce or cancel one another at various places. In the end, though we do not observe these waves. We observe, say, the impact of a photon. There! A particle, making its appearance at a specific place, say, a specific point on your retina when you see a brief flash of light. But “en route”, there was no particle. We cannot identify the path that the particle traveled in order to reach its destination because no such path exists. What we can do is explore that “probability wave” as it “travels” from source to destination. This allows us to assign specific probabilities as to where the “particle” might be observed when it comes to that. So you see… that thing we observe is really not a particle: a particle, like a miniature cannonball, would follow a well-defined trajectory, and in this case, no such trajectory exists. But that thing we observe is really not a wave either. The “wave” in question is a mathematical abstraction, a probability amplitude, not a “thing”. The “thing” is the impact of the photon on your retina, which is particle-like behavior, but again, a true particle would have a path associated with it. And it is this point that I need to offer a reminder that, like it or not, quantum physics cannot be intuited. It is outside the ability of the human mind to intuit these things, just as, say, a language model like GPT cannot “intuit” an image or a sound, as it lacks the ability to process images or sounds. It can still reason about them, but that reasoning requires discipline and, well, knowledge of mathematics. We are in the same shoes here: With our scientific discipline and mathematical tools, we can make robust predictions about the quantum world. But we make these predictions precisely because we let go of our desire to intuit the quantum world and instead, chose to follow the math (verified by experiment, of course). So that’s my advice: Do not take this “wave-particle” business literally, as an invitation to try to intuit the unintuitable. Or if you must, at least remind yourself that the “wave” is a probability wave (not a physical thing), and the “particle” is not really a particle with a definite path, even if in the end, when we observe it (but only then!) it may masquerade as one. How does a perfect fluid have a rest frame in relativity even though its different particles aren't at rest with respect to each other? First of all, in the context of relativity theory a medium such as a fluid is a continuous medium. No particles are involved. The fluid may be in motion, which is to say, to every point we can assign a velocity vector, telling us how the infinitesimally small volume of the fluid at that location moves. This means that we can also apply a “local” Lorentz transformation, which is to say, a Lorentz transformation that varies from point to point, to remove this velocity, and find the “local” rest frame of reference. A fluid is a perfect fluid if, in this frame of reference, its state is described entirely by its density and pressure: there are no stresses present. It is of course true that real fluids are not continuous mediums but consist of particles. So the perfect fluid model is only approximately valid. It is useful when it comes to describing the average, bulk properties of matter; not so useful when we look at matter at the microscopic level, where particle interactions become relevant.

Could a device be invented that synchronizes the flow of time between vastly different gravitational fields, standardizing time measurement across space? The answer is a flat no, but behind this answer lies an understanding of what time really is. I mean, in practical terms, not hifalutin’ philosophy. That is to say, what we measure as time in this one-and-only physical universe in which we, for better or for worse, live. One observed property of this physical universe is that in it there are things that tick. Not only do they tick, they tick reliably. Which is to say, if you have two such things, they will tick at the same rate. And even if you take them on distant journeys, when you bring them back together, they’ll still be ticking at the same rate. We call these things reliable clocks. It does not matter if they are cesium atoms or grandfather clocks. The only thing that matters is that they tick reliably, and they are reliably identical. Now you take two of these things and start counting the ticks. Then you let them off on different journeys. When you bring them back together, they’ll still be ticking in synch, but you will find that one may have counted fewer ticks than the other! And it depends on the journey it took. The one that traveled faster. Made more changes in speed or direction. The one that spent more time near heavy objects. Note that I have not mentioned any “flow of time” nor do I plan to, apart from this one mention on double quotes. There is no such thing. What there is, it’s a property associated with the paths of the respective trajectories of these reliable clocks: their world lines, that is. A kind of a “length” (though a rather non-intuitive concept of “length”) associated with these world lines. A reliable clock measures this length, called “proper time” along its world line. Different world lines have different lengths between the same points. But why is it surprising? After all, different paths between two points have different lengths in a map, too. Walking straight takes fewer steps than following a zig-zag path. Now I mentioned the proper time is counterintuitive, and it is true: Unlike lengths, proper time is the longest between two events when the clock is moving inertially, not accelerated in any way. Take two events. Say, right here, at my desk, at 6 PM tonight and at 6 PM tomorrow. My reliable clock counts exactly 86,400 ticks between these two events. But if you were to be here at 6 PM then blast off in your relativistic spaceship at high acceleration, turn around at some point, and get back at 6 PM tomorrow, your world line would have fewer ticks. The same thing happens in gravitational fields: a world line taking through a gravitational field will be measured with fewer ticks than another that takes a different path. Of course many other things affect the overall “length” of a world line, but this is the role gravitational fields play. In fact, reliable clocks can even be used to measure gravitational fields! (Today’s atomic clocks are sensitive enough to measure a difference in altitude amounting to no more than a few centimeters.) But ultimately, it’s not about any “flow of time” (sorry, I just broke my promise and mentioned it a second time). It’s about the “length”, i.e., the proper time associated with, different world lines. That proper time is the only actual concept of time that we can measure. Every other concept of time — e.g., coordinate time, “flow of time” (yikes! That’s the third time!) — is a mathematical or philosophical construct, not physical reality. Proper time is physical reality. In fact, ultimately all other measurements — measuring lengths, for instance, or speed — boil down to calibrating the measurements using reliable clocks and proper time in general relativity. If motion is non-absolute, why are we looking for dark energy when energy isn't required for a 'perceptually'-expanding universe? Don’t be misled by a name. “Dark energy” is neither “dark” nor “energy”. Blame physicists for coming up with inappropriate names and sticking with them long after they exhausted their usefulness. (The inappropriate names, not the physicists.) It’s called “dark” when in fact it should be called “invisible”. Or “completely transparent, not interacting with known forms of matter or light”. But… okay, “dark”. As to “energy”, well, insofar as general relativity is concerned, at least in the context of cosmology, everything is “energy”: that is, everything is characterized by its energy-content and pressure. Which is to say, everything in a non-empty universe is assumed to be well approximated by the concept of an “isotropic perfect fluid”. So “dark energy” is really a “completely transparent, non-interacting medium with negative pressure, characterized by the equation of state p = − ρ , “ which is to say, its pressure is the negative of its energy density. Contrast this with “dark matter”, which is a “completely transparent, non-interacting medium with no pressure.” Sometimes also called “dust”. Motion has nothing to do with it. The equations of cosmology match observations (in particular, minute fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background and the large-scale statistical distribution of matter) if the universe is roughly 70% “dark energy” and 30% “dust” (which also includes ordinary matter, by the way, since its pressure is negligible compared to relativistic mediums.) As to the expansion, nothing perceptual about it. Things are flying apart. Not something abstract like “the universe”, or “space” or the “cosmos”. Literally, things: galaxies, clusters of galaxies are flying apart, which is to say, the average distance between them increases over time, their density decreasing over time. Does dark matter convert into energy like baryonic matter (E=MC^2)? If so, what type of energy (not electromagnetic or dark energy)? Contrary to millions of popular accounts that suggest otherwise (usually to dazzle their readership), the equation, E = m c 2 , is absolutely not about converting anything into anything. Here is the title of Einstein’s 1905 paper that introduced this equation in its modern interpretation (the correct one, not the misunderstood reinterpretations): Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energiegehalt abhängig? (Does the Inertia of a Body Depend upon its Energy-Content, Annalen der Physik, 18:639, 1905). Let’s look at the title more closely. Inertia of course means inertial mass, the resistance of a body to acceleration. This is the mass m that appears in Newton’s second law, F = m a . Einstein’s question, which he answers affirmatively in the body of the paper, is whether the inertia of a body is determined by whatever energies are “stored” inside that body. Any by “energy”, we don’t mean anything mysterious. There really are only two types of energy worth considering. One is the energy of motion: kinetic energy. The other is the energy associated with positions (where a body is): potential energy. This is about how bodies relate to one another, attraction and repulsion and the associated energy. A special case is rest mass, which can be seen as a body interacting with itself. In quantum field theory, “particles” are in a sense illusions: what are real are the quantum fields. The quantum fields can gain energy from interacting with other quantum fields, and when they gain energy, it comes in the form of discrete lumps, “excitations”. These excitations may be detected in the right experiments as discrete particles. This is how particles are “created”. So when two quantum fields interact, their kinetic energies can transform, create new excitations, and new “particles” are born, so long as all other conservation laws are satisfied. It is not possible to create a single electron this way; that would violate charge conservation. But it is possible to create an electron-positron pair, in the right experimental setup, by allowing other fields carrying lots and lots of kinetic energy interact with the electron field (not to be confused with the electromagnetic field, the quanta of which are the photons). But it requires interaction. So moving on to dark matter: the standard “cold/collisionless dark matter”, or CDM model involves dark matter that does not interact (or if it does, only very weakly) with itself or with baryonic matter. So it does not matter how much kinetic energy is present in the form of dark matter, if it cannot transfer that energy to the Standard Model fields that constitute normal (baryonic) matter. Finally, one more comment on the terminology. The expression “dark energy” suggests some other type of energy! It is not. Words mislead us, especially when the jargon of a field or profession alters meaning. Theoretical physics has quite a few examples: the “vacuum speed of light” may not be the speed at which light travels (e.g., if we allow photons to be massive), gauge theories have nothing to do with gauges, modern particle physics is really the physics of interacting fields with “particles” only an afterthought and, well, dark energy is not energy, really, but a “perfect fluid” (which is not really fluid, lol) a medium that has uniform density and pressure with no shear or viscosity. In particular, dark energy is a perfect fluid with very large negative pressure. Not some mysterious form of “energy”, although of course, like all forms of matter, it has energy-content. Viktor T. Toth said that life on Earth is made possible by the low enthropy energy we receive from the Sun. What is meant by “low enthropy energy” and in what sense is it necessary for creating and maintaining life on Earth? As per the second law of thermodynamics, entropy cannot decrease in a closed system. Entropy is a measure of disorder: A disordered system will not spontaneously become ordered. The more disordered a system is, the higher its entropy. Life, ultimately, is about disordered raw materials combining to form complex, highly ordered structures. This represents a significant decrease in entropy. That decrease in entropy must be balanced, in turn, by an increase in entropy somewhere else, and the two systems must be connected. That somewhere else is the Sun. The Earth receives, from the Sun, energy mostly in the form of visible light, photons at (roughly) 6000 K (degrees kelvin). In turn, the Earth radiates into deep space energy mostly in the form of thermal infrared, photons at (roughly) 300 K. That means that for each incoming photon from the Sun, the Earth radiates about 20 photons into deep space. (The two must be in balance otherwise the Earth would boil or freeze, due to excess thermal energy or a deficit in thermal energy.) It goes without saying that 20 photons can represent a lot more disorder, a lot more randomness than 1 photon. In other words, the energy that the Earth receives from the Sun has a lot less entropy than the thermal “waste heat” that the Earth radiates into deep space. Some of the incoming solar energy is captured by living things, either directly (plants) or indirectly (e.g., humans eating a potato). This represents a low entropy source, allowing those living systems to become organized, create complexity, and radiate away excess energy in the form of higher entropy waste heat. But it need not be even about living things. Just imagine a simple machine that uses the heat from the Sun to boil water, which then drives a piston, which does useful work through a mechanism (e.g., a crane, lifting bricks to build a house, turning disorder into order). The used up steam, released from the piston, is allowed to recondense, its waste heat radiated into the sky (deep space), the water ready to be reused in the next cycle. If there was no “high entropy sink” (the sky), we could not recondense the water and the machine would eventually stop when its water reservoir is emptied. The biological cycle may be a tad more sophisticated than a simple solar steam engine driving a crane, but the thermodynamic principles are exactly the same. If space is expanding (or perhaps 'stretching' is a better verb) at a rate we call the Hubble Constant (or thereabouts), at what rate is time expanding (in seconds per kilometer per petasecond - s/km/Ps)? You stumbled upon one of the silliest, most persistent misunderstandings concerning cosmology. No, space is not expanding. Nor is it contracting or dancing the tango. Or perhaps it does… if it did, we would not know. Space does not have little markers attached to it by which it could be measured. Space is not a physical entity that would carry energy or momentum. In short, space is not a thing. But, but… cosmic expansion! The Friedmann equations! The Hubble-parameter! Well… the famous Friedmann equations, which also define the Hubble parameter, represent a specific application of Einstein’s field equations, for the case of a cosmos that is filled with matter such that the distribution is homogeneous in space (i.e., uniform density) and isotropic (no preferred direction). But… Einstein’s field equations! It’s all about the bending of space and time! Er… Not really. There are two things in Einstein’s field equations: The gravitational field, represented by a so-called tensor quantity, and the energy-momentum of matter, also represented by a tensor quantity. It is true that Einstein’s field equations can be interpreted geometrically. So what? We can also interpret electromagnetism using geometry (just ask Weyl, or consider how the electromagnetic interaction is introduced through a covariant derivative in quantum electrodynamics.) What makes gravity special is that matter is introduced into the equations solely through its energy-momentum; what the stuff is made of makes no difference. This, namely the so-called weak equivalence principle, implies that the geometry we see is the only geometry that can be measured. In contrast, in the case of electromagnetism the geometry that we see depends on the charge-to-mass ratio of the object used to measure it, so there is no one-and-only, unique geometry. (I shall refrain from quoting Einstein himself again, as I’ve already done so many times in the past here on Quora, arguing against taking the geometric interpretation, which he called a mental aid, too literally, too dogmatically.) Anyhow, back to cosmology. What those Friedmann equations tell us is how the gravitational field changes on the one hand, and how the density of matter changes at the same time. If we think of matter as particles, that implies that the characteristic distance between particles changes over time. This characteristic distance can also be thought of as part of geometry, thus characterize the gravitational field itself. But, I stress, the geometry part is interpretation. The actual, physical things in the equation are matter and the gravitational field. In the standard form in which the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric (i.e., the gravitational field) is written, we have d s 2 = c 2 d t 2 − a ( t ) 2 d R 2 , where a ( t ) is the time-dependent “scale factor”. When it is applied to a universe dominated by matter with little or no pressure (that is, ordinary nonrelativistic matter, or also “cold dark matter”) that a ( t ) indeed serves well as the measure by which the typical distance between particle changes over time. Note that time itself does not have a factor like that. And a ( t ) ceases to be a valid measure of this change of density if the matter in question is not predominantly “pressureless dust”. Which, incidentally, is already the case today, as (at least according to the prevailing ΛCDM cosmological model) about 70% of matter in the present universe is “dark energy”, stuff with large negative pressure, the density of which remains constant over time. But putting all that aside: In terms of actual, observable effects, what we see of course is that light from distant objects is shifted in frequency. For objects relatively close to our Milky Way galaxy, this shift in frequency is mainly a velocity-induced Doppler frequency shift, as those objects are receding from us (or we, from them). But for objects that are very far from here, high-redshift objects, the dominant contribution to the redshift is gravitational, which can be thought of as a result of changing gravitational time dilation as the average gravitational field in the distant past (when matter was more dense) was greater than it is today. As to the Hubble parameter, it kind of captures both effects (it is defined as H = ˙ a / a where the dot represents differentiation with respect to time) but keep in mind that it is not really a constant at all; as its definition itself implies, since a ( t ) is a function of time, so is H ( t ) . I know, I know, this is not the kind of simple, concise answer that you might have hoped for. But I am trying to follow Einstein’s advice: Make things as simple as possible but no simpler. Relativistic cosmology may not be the most complicated subject in modern physics, but that does not mean it is easy to grasp or always intuitive.
