Does Victor Toth agree that his explanation of the cosmic microwave background with the help of pops on the square is more suitable for "substantiating" the Olbers paradox? A strange question but certainly not a silly one! First, a reminder. I used the “pops on the square” analogy to explain why light from a single instance of time (the moment of time confusingly called the “surface of last scattering” when the cosmic microwave background originated) is seen as continuous radiation. To recap: You are in a very, very, very large square, full of people as far as the eye can see and beyond. Something happens, say, a flash in the sky, and simultaneously, everyone claps once. But that is not what you hear. The moment it occurs, you hear clapping nearby. A second later, you hear the clapping from people roughly 1000 feet away beause sound travels at a finite speed. Sure, the sound diminishes with distance but there are also more people along a circle of 1000 feet in radius than nearby, so the total intensity doesn’t really diminish that much. At two seconds, you hear clapping from even more people at 2000 feet away. At 10 seconds, it’s the folks at 10,000 feet. And so on. If the square is infinitely large, the clapping never stops. This is why we continue seeing cosmic background radiation. Granted, it’s faster, but Just like sound, light also travels at a finite speed. Today, we see light (well, microwave radiation) from volumes of gas at 13.8 billion light years (light travel distance); tomorrow, we’ll see it from volumes of gas situated at 13.8 billion light years and one light day away. How does this relate to Olbers’s Paradox? The 19th century German astronomer Olbers asked a simple question: If space is infinite, and there are stars everywhere, no matter which direction we look in the sky, eventually that direction should terminate on the surface of some distant star. So why is the night sky dark? The answer, of course, is that we do not live in an eternal universe. The universe has a finite age. No matter what direction we look, eventually we run out of stars: the oldest star cannot be older than the universe itself, so beyond 13.8 billion light years, there are no more stars. Given the density of stars in the universe, that means that in most sky directions, we don’t see any stars at all. There is more to the story of course because in an expanding universe, distant stars are also dimmer as they are receding from us, but we don’t even need expansion to understand the key argument: Olbers’s paradox works only in an eternal universe. Back to my example of the clapping crowd in the square: It’s different. The folks in the crowd are not clapping continuously. The clapping is a single event. But you know what? Let’s assume a square in which folks are clapping continuously, and have always been clapping. That means that at any moment in time, you hear clapping from all of them. Nearby claps that happen now; distant claps that happened seconds, minutes, hours earlier, with the sound only reaching your ear now. If the square is truly infinite, that means that at any given moment in time, you are subjected to noise from an infinite number of people. There, Olbers’s paradox. But wait… people. People don’t live forever. Say, everyone in this imaginary square is exactly 20 years old. They have been clapping all their lives, since they were born. So that means that you hear clapping from as far away as, well, over 600 billion feet, so this is truly not realistic of course, just a thought experiment, but the point is, you get a lot of clapping, but no clapping sound reaches your ears from beyond 600 billion feet, give or take. Why? Because there were no people alive, doing any clapping in this square, more than 20 years ago! From places in the square more distant than 600 billion feet, the earliest clapping sounds have not had a chance to reach you just that! Okay, I know, I am stretching an already weird, silly analogy but still. I hope it answers the question, any possible relationship between Olbers’s paradox (which explains why the night sky is not as bright as the Sun) vs. the cosmic microwave background (which shines from all sky directions and never stops.) From an outside observers point of view, a black hole never forms. The rest of the universe is an outside observer. So how can Hawking radiation ever escape to the outside universe? As others pointed out, the popular account of Hawking radiation — a pair of particles popping into existence near the event horizon, one with positive one with negative energy, the negative energy particle being “eaten” by the horizon while the other escapes — is dead wrong. In fact, we can suspect this much simply by looking at the basic features of Hawking radiation. Its characteristic wavelength is about 20 times (!) the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole. That alone should make it fairly obvious that Hawking radiation doesn’t really come from the horizon proper. Indeed, when we actually look at Hawking’s own 1974 paper (rather than his popular book) a very different picture emerges. Hawking radiation is deduced from a so-called semiclassical description of quantum fields: that is to say, quantum field theory in the curved spacetime background of general relativity. This curved spacetime background is not static. An astrophysical black hole is in a perpetual state of collapse. This creates an asymmetry between past and future. When we extend the quantum fields using the appropriate “past infinity” and “future infinity” boundary conditions, the resulting configuration is not symmetric. This yields an outgoing flow of radiation, which is what Hawking radiation really is. This radiation originates from the neighborhood of the gravitating object, and it is a result of the “gravitational vacuum polarization” that is produced by the object’s gravitational field. The presence of a horizon is not essential to this process, nor does the radiation originate from, or from within, the horizon. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is it true or false that the general theory of relativity predicts light should go straight down into a black hole whereas advanced quantum mechanics predicts that there should be a swirling torrent of gamma rays around a blackhole called a firewall? Not exactly. In general relativity, a black hole is eternal. In fact, to outside observers its formation process takes forever. (The first paper that seriously explored this topic, the famous Oppenheimer-Snyder paper from 1939, is titled “On Continued Gravitational Contraction”). Anything that gets trapped by the formation process, including rays of light, remains trapped forever. Then there is the semiclassical picture, that makes a connection between classical general relativity and quantum field theory. Granted, it does not include a quantized theory of gravitation as no such theory exists (yet?) but it is also not needed. In the vicinity of an astrophysical black hole quantum gravity effects, if any, remain negligible. What the semiclassical picture tells us is that in the vicinity of an object, in a state of “continued contraction”, gravitational vacuum polarization produces outgoing radiation. This outgoing radiation is extremely weak and low in frequency. (The characteristic wavelength is about 20 times the black hole’s Schwarzschild radius.) So it takes an insane number of years (a number with as many as 70 or more digits) for the entire mass-energy of the collapsing object to be converted into radiation. But it’s all there. An outside observer could, in principle, watch an infalling object, never quite reaching the horizon even after that 70-digit number of years, all the while encountering this very weak Hawking radiation. But due to extreme relativistic time dilation, to the infalling object the process may only take seconds! So it encounters the same amount of energy in the form of Hawking radiation, but not as very weak radiation over an insane number of years but as a blast of radiation compressed to mere seconds. [Just to be clear though, the black hole firewall proposal goes beyond this, and proposes a blast of radiation to resolve what is known as the information loss paradox. That is not a subject I wish to touch in this answer, though.] Anyhow, a ray of light still goes down into a black hole, quantum physics or no quantum physics. The main difference is that if Hawking radiation is taken seriously, the black hole is not eternal; its lifespan is finite. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

At moment 0 in the Lambda CDM model, is there any speculation (speculation, of course, but commonly held belief) as to whether there was anything (matter/energy) "adjacent" to the singularity that became the observable universe? There is no “moment 0” in the standard cosmological (Lambda-CDM) model. It’s indeed a “singularity”. Which is a mathematical concept, best illustrated by a simple function that is singular, say, y = 1 / x 2 . That function exists for all values of x except for x = 0. You can get as close to x = 0 as you want. But at x = 0 , the function does not exist. The value x = 0 is not part of its domain. Similarly, t = 0 is not part of the domain of the standard cosmological model and its spacetime. You can get as close to it as you want. A second. A picosecond. The Planck time. The Planck time divided by a very big number. Whatever it is, it has to be finite and greater than zero: that is, in the standard cosmology, t > 0 , not t ≥ 0. We can speculate anything we want about the value t = 0 , therefore, but it’s science-fiction, with emphasis on the fiction part, not science. Also, I should stress that the actual science of physical cosmology begins with the present (which we observe) and extrapolates our knowledge into the past, but only as far as we can, not farther. The farthest to which we can legitimately extrapolate our knowledge is roughly t = 10 − 12 seconds, when conditions were similar to the high-energy particle collisions in the LHC. Anything prior to this time is pure speculation already; indeed, we don’t even necessarily know for sure if that picosecond was a picosecond or an eternity. Can you explain why the pressure inside of a black hole becomes infinite? The interior solution describing a collapsing astrophysical object turns out to be the same set of equations that would describe a collapsing cosmos. A hapless observer who found himself falling into a black hole, after crossing the event horizon, would find himself in such a collapsing “mini-Universe”. Depending on the size of this mini-Universe (determined by the amount of matter that fell, and will ever fall, into it), it may take anywhere from a millisecond to many hours, but the mini-Universe collapses. The observer would not live to see this, as ever increasing tidal forces would rip his body apart before the end. But that end (at least for a spherically symmetric black hole) inevitably happens: the famed “singularity” is not some bad spot that you can bypass by clever maneuvering, but a future moment in time at which (insofar as this mini-Universe is concerned) time itself comes to an end. So it’s not so much that pressure, density, etc., become infinite at this moment but rather, this moment literally is not part of existence: Whatever is inside the mini-Universe ceases to exist at this point. For outside observers, however, none of this ever happens. Even the event horizon itself remains forever in their future. Only by falling through it can the event horizon be experienced. That is the “classical” picture anyway. If we account for quantum physics, the answer is, we don’t really know what happens. In the absence of a quantum gravity theory, we can only take educated guesses, invoking what is known as the “semiclassical approximation”. One possibility (if you asked me, I think it’s the most likely one) is that the collapse never even happens as the black hole evaporates before its event horizon forms. In which case, there is no “inside” at all. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why would Americans rather drive their car for days than take the train? I live in Ottawa, Canada. I occasionally visit New York City. Google Maps tells me that I could depart tomorrow at 6:07 AM and arrive in Montreal at 8:11 AM. Three hours later, I would depart on Amtrak's Adirondack train, which could deliver me at Penn station a mere 11 hours later, at 10:15 PM. OK, how about return? Do gravitational waves experience redshift with expansion of the gravitational field, like photons in the EM field? Indeed they do. But don't think of it as gravitational waves "experiencing" anything. Neither gravitationl waves, nor light "experience" anything as they travel in an expanding spacetime from a source to a detector. They do not exchange energy, momentum, or angular momentum with their environment. Nothing happens to them, as a matter of fact. However, as a distant observer, chances are that you are moving at high speed relative to the source of these waves. This will certainly produce a Doppler effect: Each subsequent crest of the wave will have to travel slightly longer to reach you, so the interval between them will increase. Moreover, the waves may originate in the distant past, when the universe was denser and the average gravitational potential was greater. That means significant gravitational time dilation: Clocks of the past were ticking slower than clocks of the present, so a wave emitted at a given frequency back then will appear to have a lower frequency today. It is this combination of expansion-related Doppler and gravitational time dilation that are together responsible for the observed cosmological redshift in an expanding universe. Can a wave length of a wave be changed? I mean from gamma rays or x-rays to change (by changing the wave length) into ultraviolet waves, radio waves, etc. The wavelength of light is not an intrinsic property. It depends on the observer. Want to change a wavelength? Run towards the source and it will appear shorter. Run away from the source and it will be longer. (Doppler blue- or redshift). Gravity works, too. But what you need to change is the relationship between the clocks characterizing the emitter vs. the clocks characterizing the detector. That is because wavelength (talking about electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, to be clear) is inversely proportional to frequency, i.e., the number of wave crests and troughs per second. Wave crests and troughs do not get created or destroyed en route, so the only way to change the observed wavelength (i.e., frequency) is by either changing the rate at which you receive them (moving towards, or away from, the source can do that) or by changing the rate at which your clock ticks compared to the clock at the emitter (movement contributes to this, too, due to special relativity; gravity as well, due to general relativity.) Of course you can always do something the old-fashioned way and put something in the way of that light: a transparent material with a refractive index will of course change wavelength, by altering the speed at which the wave travels. Is it sexist that women are not being selected to win a Nobel Prize? Could it be that the work of those women do not measure to the actual work the winners of the awards have accomplished? Here's a quote from a recent video by Sabine Hossenfelder: [...] I wasn’t offered a job because I’m a woman. I'm not guessing that that’s what happened, I know, because they told me. You see, the guy who was head of the institute told me that, since I'm female I should apply for a scholarship that was exclusively for women in the natural sciences. Because then the institute wouldn't have to pay for me. I met Sabine (at the Perimeter Institute). My impression was that she radiated self-confident knowledge and competence. To the extent I am qualified to judge, she came across as a very sensible, good physicist with a well-earned reputation, who has put a lot on the table in her career as a professional physicist, and who would never pull the “gender card” to complain. The situation she describes sounds awfully familiar, probably repeated far too often at universities and research institutes around the world, even today. Women face a multitude of obstacles, starting with the cultural: the “hard” sciences are often presented as male pursuits, whereas women should supposedly be more interested in, I don’t know, arts, crafts, or raising babies. I suspect that this already discourages far too many talented young women. Then there is human biology: the birth of a child can burden any parent, but the burden is obviously disproportionately the mother’s, starting with pregnancy and childbirth itself. Family expectations may pile on top of cultural stereotypes: The young mother may be expected to stay at home with the children, while the father assumes the traditional role of breadwinner. Obstacles like that which Sabine encountered may not even be based on downright gender prejudice. Institutions may simply be worried that hiring a woman is like playing the lottery: The woman may get pregnant, perhaps multiple times, absent from her position for extended periods of time. But yes, old-fashioned, ugly gender prejudice is likely still present at times, not to mention unacceptable behavior like harassment or worse. I recall a discussion I once had with someone, about Sabine: the person I was conversing with questioned her competence, unfavorably comparing her to a much younger (male, of course) physicist who has not yet published anything notable at the time. It was clear to me that I was witnessing an outburst of classic, old-fashioned sexism. And it doesn’t take much to change the statistic. When you look at Nobel laureates, they represent an extreme, one of the trailing ends of the Gaussian curve characterizing the scientific community. All it takes is a small shift of the curve to the left, barely noticeable in its central part, for there to be an order-of-magnitude difference near the trailing ends. In short, even if I boldly assume that we no longer need to worry about gender bias in the Nobel selection process that may have deprived the likes of Lise Meitner, Emmy Noether, Cecilia Payne, Jocelyn Bell Burnell, Vera Rubin or Chien-Shiung Wu, just to name a few examples (if the names are unfamiliar, look them up, it’s worth your time), of well-deserved recognition, the cards are still far too often stacked against women by both biology and society. Writing this reminded me of one of my heroes, a person who surely would have deserved a Nobel prize, if only computer scientists qualified for one. I am of course talking about the amazing Grace Hopper, mathematician, computer scientist, and rear admiral of the United States Navy, at the time of her retirement the oldest serving commissioned officer in the armed forces of the United States. One of the things she is known for may not be universally liked but it is still widely in use today, nearly 65 years after its invention: The COBOL programming language.

What are the 'rays' (not animals), or 'beams of radiation' that are not ElectroMagnetic radiation? In the context of radioactivity, historically there have been three types of radiation considered, only one of which is electromagnetic: Speaking of electromagnetic radiation, radio waves including microwaves (yes, in your microwave oven), infrared radiation, visible light, ultraviolet radiation, X-rays and gamma rays are all electromagnetic radiation. (I listed them in the order of increasing frequency, which means increasing energy, decreasing wavelength. It’s these categories that people think about when they mention the “electromagnetic spectrum”.) After the alpha-beta-gamma categories were established, it was recognized that some radioactive elements emitted electrically neutral neutrons, so that’s another form of non-electromagnetic radiation. Then there are neutrinos, emitted, e.g., by nuclear reactors; they interact very weakly, so they are almost undetectable, although in stellar catastrophes, supernova explosions, an incredible neutrino flux plays a major role in how these astronomical explosions unfold. And there are also gravitational waves, including those that we detected, emitted during the final moments of black hole and neutron star mergers. Again, not electromagnetic.

How can virtual particles become real particles e.g. while Hawking radiation? I suspect that this question was at least inspired by the popular, but fundamentally misleading “explanation” that Hawking radiation is about the creation of virtual particle-antiparticle pairs near the horizon, one of which is swallowed by the horizon, while the other is released as a “real” particle. This explanation, though it first appeared I believe in Hawking’s own popular science book, is nonetheless nonsensical, in direct contradiction with Hawking’s own 1974 paper (Nature 248 (5443)), which explains how gravitational vacuum polarization, along with the past-future asymmetry of a system in a perpetual state of collapse, leads to a net outgoing radiation. But I suspect there is also a misunderstanding here concerning the nature of particles, be they real or virtual, in the context of quantum field theory. Take the electromagnetic field. The classical theory is Maxwell’s: it’s a field theory, which is to say, it describes something that is present everywhere, with a continuously varying value from point to point in space and time. This field may be sourced by electric charges. If charges are absent, the field equations can still have nonzero solutions, which are in the form of plane waves traveling at constant velocity (the velocity that we know as the vacuum speed of light). When it comes to the quantum theory, we start with decomposing the field into elementary frequencies, kind of like how a sound can be decomposed into elementary pure sounds of different pitch. Each of these pure waves can be treated as a “harmonic oscillator”, which, in the quantum theory, has discrete levels of energy. It is these discrete levels, or packets, of energy that will be the field quanta, and it is these quanta that we perceive, under the right circumstances, as particles. When we write down the equations of fields, especially interacting fields, the equations include nasty summations (integrals) of ever more complicated interactions. As a mental aid, however, we can think of these interactions in terms of one unit, one quantum at a time, and even use neat little diagrams (the Feynman diagrams) as a bookkeeping device, keeping track of these terms. The arrows in that Feynman diagram are suggestive of particle-like behavior. Even though no actual particles are involved, it can sometimes be helpful to intuit these interactions as exchanges of “virtual particles”. Unfortunately intuition in particle physics is a dangerous business. Helpful, yes, but do not forget for a moment that these are merely bookkeeping devices. There are no miniature cannonballs, virtual or otherwise. Only interacting fields. The “particle” aspect is entirely imaginary, existing only in our heads, as a clumsy mental aid to help our limited intuition. That’s what “virtual” really means.

Is gravity a force or a space? If it's not a force, then why is it measured in Newton? If it's a curved spacetime, then why isn't it measured in Einstein, or in curved metersecond? First of all, let us settle the basic question. Is gravity a force? It is, of course, fashionable to dazzle laypersons with the pronouncement that “Einstein proved that gravity is not a force, it’s the warping of spacetime!” But some folks disagree. Here’s my favorite (though by no means only) quote on the subject: “It is wrong to think that 'geometrization' is something essential. It is only a kind of crutch (Eselsbrücke) for the finding of numerical laws. Whether one links 'geometrical' intuitions with a theory is a ... private matter.” (“Es ist verkehrt zu glauben, dass die 'Geometrisierung' etwas Wesentliches bedeutet. Es ist nur eine Art Eselsbrücke zur Auffindung numerischer Gesetze. Ob man mit einer Theorie 'geometrische' Vorstellungen verbindet, ist [unleserlich] Privatsache.”) The gent who wrote these words back in 1926? Why, his name was A. Einstein. (Einstein to Reichenbach, 8 April 1926, as quoted by Lehmkuhl, Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326.) Now let me elaborate a little bit on the “gravity is not a force” business. It is not completely silly, after all. The geometric interpretation of gravity looks at freely falling reference frames as the gravitational generalization of inertial frames. What happens when you are in a noninertial frame? You feel fictitious forces, like the centrifugal force. When you stand on the ground, you are in a noninertial frame: The ground prevents you from falling. So from this perspective, gravity may be viewed as a fictitious force, or pseudoforce. However, there is a crucial difference. Pseudoforces are not associated with real, physical fields. However, the gravitational field is a real, physical field. Like the electromagnetic field, it has its own independent existence. Gravitational waves can carry influences, energy and momentum, from place to place the same way electromagnetic waves can. The gravitational force, whether or not we interpret it using geometry, corresponds to how the gravitational field, this real, tangible, physical field changes from place to place. Not to mention that if we insist on doing geometry, it is eminently possible to reinterpret electromagnetism using geometry! And no, I don’t even mean the “old school” attempts at geometrizing electromagnetism, like Weyl’s “linear groundform”, Kaluza-Klein theory in 5 dimensions, or Einstein’s attempt to unify gravity and electromagnetism using a nonsymmetric tensor field. No, I mean quantum electrodynamics: how the contribution of electromagnetism is captured in an eminently geometric object, the covariant derivative. Except… except that in this case, the geometry depends on the “charge-to-mass ratio” of the object at hand. An object that is heavy with little or no charge behaves differently from an object that is light and has a lot of charge. Gravity is not like this: the “charge” (gravitational mass) is the same as the (inertial) mass, so the ratio is always exactly 1. Therefore, the geometry is unique, not dependent on the object’s material properties. This may explain why the geometric interpretation of gravity is so very popular! Popular but all too often deeply misunderstood. Recall those wonderful rubber-sheet illustrations of how gravity curves space? Garbage. Seriously. That is because the part that corresponds to Newtonian gravity in general relativity has nothing to do with space. It has to do with time. Between any two events (not locations! Events: specific locations at specific moments in time) along the worldline of a freely falling object, the object follows a trajectory that maximizes time. In special relativity, this would be a straight line (inertial motion); in general relativity, the results are the well-known Keplerian orbits, at least up to a very good approximation. Curvature of space comes in as a second-order effect; here on the surface of the Earth, it’s a tiny, roughly one-part-in-a-billion correction. So yes, gravity is very much a force, its geometric interpretation notwithstanding. Like any force, it is measured in the SI system of units using newtons (when used as a unit, the word is not capitalized). Then again, pseudoforces are also measured in newtons, so even if we “buy into” the geometric interpretation, the unit of measurement would remain the same: it measures a force, which is acceleration times mass. Why do people who use the metric system assume that 9meters is 32 feet when gravity is really 9.81m per sec per sec? Well, for starters, “gravity” is not really 9.81 m/s^2. What is 9.81 m/s^2 is the average gravitational acceleration at sea level on a minor planet called Earth in one of the popular languages spoken by its inhabitants. The units in this expression were historically derived from the actual properties of the same planet (notably, its size and its rate of rotation) but that’s beside the point. In a small number of places on this planet, however, inhabitants prefer to use a different unit for length, originally inspired by the typical size of one of their appendages they call “feet”. The conversion factor is a simple one: 1 foot equals 0.3048 meters or conversely, 1 m = (1/0.3048) ft. The rest is easily done by way of using a calculator: 9.81 m / s^2 = 9.81 (1/0.3048) ft / s^2 = 9.81/0.3048 ft / s^2 = 32.2 ft / s^2, rounded to three significant digits in the decimal number system these inhabitants prefer (undoubtedly because their forepaws happen to have ten appendages in total, called “digits”). This simple calculation should not challenge any of the adult or near-adult inhabitants of the aforementioned planet, whether or not they are regular users of what they call the metric system or other systems of measurement. Utilizing the same skills and a calculating device, they can also easily calculate that 9 m = (9 / 0.3048) ft = 29.527559 ft to a reasonable number of decimal digits. Indeed, most of the inhabitants master the necessary skill set in an institution called “grade school”. Yes, I know, strange planet. How do you know there is no speed of gravity? For the same reason I know there is no speed of water. I look at a glass of water, and it’s perfectly still. I look at a fast-flowing river, and the water is moving, well, very fast. I look the icy moon Europa of the planet Jupiter, and I see tremendous quantities of water ice moving very, very fast around Jupiter. Or maybe not moving at all if I happened to stand on Europa’s icy surface? So what exactly is the speed of water? On the other hand, I do know, for instance, the speed at which certain influences travel in water. Though it is affected by things such as temperature or salinity, sound travels roughly 1.5 kilometers a second in water. That is true in the glass of water I hold in my hands, it is true in the rivers and oceans, it is even true on Europa. So then, gravity. A static gravitational field has no speed. Why would it? Speed measures change. There is no change when the field is static. However, if you are wondering how fast changes in the gravitational field travel, far from any specific source of gravitation: Why, it’s the same speed at which changes in the electromagnetic field travel, far from any sources (electric charges). It’s called the vacuum speed of light, light being the word we associate with a particular range of frequencies of electromagnetic waves, which also include radio waves, infrared and ultraviolet light, X-rays and gamma rays. Similarly, changes in the gravitational field travel in the form of waves, and far away from sources (masses), those waves are transverse waves traveling at the same vacuum speed of light. But that is not the “speed of gravity” any more than the speed of light is the “speed of electromagnetism”. Forgive the pedantry here, but it is important to convey the correct impression: namely that speed is associated with the rate at which changes travel, the static field itself has no speed associated with it.

Can you explain the concept of dark energy in the Big Bang theory? Is it considered a part of inflation? Not precisely part of inflation, but related. The standard cosmological model assumes a universe that is the same everywhere (homogeneous) and has no preferred direction (isotropic). All forms of “matter” (and by “matter”, we mean anything and everything that’s not empty space) would be in the form of “isotropic perfect fluids”: that is to say, mediums that are characterized by its mass density ρ and pressure p . The ratio of energy density and pressure is a pure number: w = p / c 2 ρ . This “equation of state” characterizes the medium. The number w can be anything between -1 and +1 (yes, this includes negative pressure). It is substantially different from zero only for “relativistic” forms of matter: ordinary matter is well described by w = 0 , which is to say, its pressure is much, much less than its energy density. (Values below -1 would yield an unstable universe; values over +1 would yield a speed of sound that exceeds the vacuum speed of light, violating causality.) So then, the question becomes: What mixture of such perfect fluids yield the observed properties of the universe? When we take the totality of observations into account, we find that observable results — including the cosmic microwave background, its minute fluctuations, the large-scale distribution of matter, the luminosity-redshift relationship of Type Ia supernovae, and a host of other observations — can be best modeled if the universe is assumed to be “spatially flat”, with 30% of all matter in the form of w = 0 “dust”, and 70% in the form of w = − 1 “dark energy”. Ordinary matter amounts to only about 4%, so the remaining 26% of “dust” is assumed to be something invisible, dubbed “dark matter”. Though there are plenty of theories, we have no idea what either of these “dark” things really are; the names are basically placeholders representing our ignorance. There is a curious point concerning matter with significant, relativistic pressure. For ordinary matter, its gravitation is determined by the mass density ρ . However, when relativistic pressure is present, it must be included as a source of gravitation: we end up with ρ + 3 p / c 2 as the source. For dark energy, w = − 1 , this implies that gravitation will be proportional to − 2 ρ , that is to say, it is repulsive! This is why the presence of dark energy actually pushes stuff in distant parts of the universe away from each other, accelerating the rate at which the universe continues to expand. Note that this is not inflation. However, inflation is related. It was supposed to happen in the very early universe, when something akin to dark energy dominated the universe, accelerating its expansion for a very brief but significant period of time. Whatever was the source of that large negative pressure, however, is supposed to have undergone some kind of phase transition, its negative pressure vanishing. Afterwards, the rate of expansion began to decrease and continued to decrease for roughly 9 billion years, before (ordinary and dark) matter became sufficiently dilute so that dark energy became dominant, and the rate of expansion began to increase again. Bottom line: though the mechanisms are closely related, do not confuse inflation (rapid expansion in the extreme early universe) with acceleration (the universe slowly shifting from a decelerating to an accelerating rate of expansion in the past 4–5 billion years). In 3 dimensions, Cartesian coordinate systems are distinguishable from their mirror images. What is the situation in 3+1 dimensions and how many inequivalent images are there? Spacetime, with its three spatial dimensions and one temporal dimension, has two “mirror” symmetries: parity and time reversal. Parity is what you get when you look at things in a mirror. Time reversal is what you get when you play the movie backwards, so to speak. These things become important in particle physics. Most of our laws of physics remain unchanged under a parity transformation: You cannot tell if you are watching an actual physics experiment or its mirror image, as they both obey the same set of equations. But there are some exceptions; e.g., neutrinos and their mirror images are not equivalent. Similarly, most of the laws of physics are the same under time reversal: When we look at particle interactions, for instance, you cannot tell if the movie is being played normally or backwards, as the same equations apply in both cases. But again, there are subtle exceptions. An important result is that when we simultaneously form a mirror image, play the movie backwards, and replace particles with antiparticles, the results are indistinguishable from reality. The laws of nature are invariant under a CPT (charge-parity-time) transformation. But what about thermodynamics, you might wonder? Entropy picks a direction of time that cannot be reversed! True. But the underlying laws of nature are still CPT symmetric. What sets the direction of entropy are initial or boundary conditions. If we set up a physical system in a low entropy initial state and leave its final state unconstrained, it will evolve from low to high entropy, even though the laws governing any individual particle are symmetric under time reversal. As far as we know, the early state of our own universe was such a low entropy state, and the future of our universe is unconstrained. Hence, we have an “arrow of time” despite the fact that physics is governed by fundamental laws that are invariant under a CPT transformation. According to general relativity theory, is there a reason for matter bend space? Are there any new discoveries at that? No, there isn’t, and it doesn’t. Before I continue, let me quote a gentleman who knew a thing or two about general relativity: “Sie haben vollständig recht. Es ist verkehrt zu glauben, dass die 'Geometrisierung' etwas Wesentliches bedeutet. Es ist nur eine Art Eselsbrücke zur Auffindung numerischer Gesetze. Ob man mit einer Theorie 'geometrische' Vorstellungen verbindet, ist [unleserlich] Privatsache.” — “You are perfectly right. It is wrong to think that the "geometrization" has significant meaning. It is only a kind of a clue helping us find numerical laws. Whether you connect a 'geometric' view to a theory is entirely a private matter.” The gent in question was a certain A. Einstein, in a letter written to a fellow named Reichenbach on April 8, 1926, as quoted by Lehmkuhl (Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics, Volume 46, Part B, May 2014, Pages 316-326.) In short: Do not take the geometric interpretation of general relativity literally or dogmatically. That does not mean it’s a bad or useless interpretation. On the contrary! And there is a darn good reason why this interpretation makes sense: the weak equivalence principle. According to the weak equivalence principle, all material objects are accelerated by gravity the same way, regardless of their composition. But this also means that if you are freely falling, surrounded by other objects, those other objects will either fall at the same rate (so they are motionless relative to you) or they move in a straight line, at uniform velocity, in your freely falling reference frame. In other words, if your happen to be inside a windowless chamber, you can never tell if you are freely falling in a gravitational field or just floating in empty space. But this also implies that a geometric transformation exists between the two cases. Or that conversely, the effects of gravitation can be effectively neutralized by a clever geometric transformation. Which implies, on the other hand, that a geometric theory that can deal with accelerating reference frames can also serve as a theory of gravitation. This was the essence of Einstein’s insight, his happiest moment, and it is more or less how the general theory of relativity was born. Yet he himself cautioned against taking this geometric interpretation too far, too literally. He never stopped referring to gravitation as a force and with good reason. You see, if we want to take the next theoretical step and perhaps… maybe unify gravity with the other forces (Einstein spent the last few decades of his life trying to construct a theory unifying classical electromagnetism and gravity). Maybe developing a quantum field theory of gravitation. Maybe exploring gravity beyond general relativity, constructing a modified gravity theory to account for some oddities in galaxy dynamics or cosmology… a dogmatic, geometric interpretation becomes an insurmountable obstacle. So no, matter does not “bend space”. We wouldn’t even know if it did; space does not have little markers or other means by which its bending could be measured. (Or time. The effects of Newtonian gravity are primarily temporal, not spatial, in the metric.) But the gravitational field of matter does alter how we measure the geometric relationships between events in space-time because everything, including all our measurements, is subject to gravity, in accordance with the weak equivalence principle. What is the equation that states that an object's observed mass increases with its velocity? There is no equation that states that an object’s observed mass changes with its velocity. Rest mass is an intrinsic property of any object and it is invariant unless the object interacts (exchanges mass-energy) with some other object. Unfortunately, especially in older texts about special relativity, there used to be this very misleading, incorrect application of the famous E = m c 2 equation, suggesting that, when an object is in motion, its kinetic energy should be added to its energy-content, increasing its mass by the famous factor 1 / √ 1 − v 2 / c 2 . This is patent nonsense. Unlike rest mass, which is an intrinsic property, kinetic energy depends on the observer. What is the kinetic energy of your luggage next to you when you are on a moving train? Why, it’s zero in your reference frame. It’s nonzero in the station’s reference frame, and even larger (a lot larger) in a heliocentric reference frame. So which value is its “mass”? The answer: none of the above. Because you see, E = m c 2 is only valid in an object’s rest frame of reference. In reference frames in which the object is moving, the correct expression is E 2 = ( m c 2 ) 2 + ( p c ) 2 where p is the object’s momentum. Conversely, m = √ ( E / c 2 ) 2 − ( p / c ) 2 is the object’s rest mass. And this value of m is the same for all observers, regardless of their motion relative to the object. As I said, it’s an invariant. But it’s only in the object’s rest frame, where p = 0 , that we get back E = m c 2 . If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Einstein believed quantum mechanics wasn’t fundamental and there must be a deeper theory. Was he correct? Well… yes and no, but context is all-important here. Einstein passed away in 1955. At the time, modern quantum field theory was still in its infancy. Yang-Mills theory that proved fundamental to the development of the Standard Model was just a few months old. In any case, I doubt Einstein had more than a very superficial familiarity with then-recent developments. The quantum mechanics that he was familiar with was basically quantum particle theory, characterized by the Schrödinger equation or maybe the relativistic Dirac equation, which were predominantly interpreted in accordance with the Copenhagen school as equations that yield a probability amplitude. Quite clearly, Einstein was not comfortable with physics that yielded only probabilities. Moreover, the Copenhagen interpretation assigns a role to the “observer”, which is fundamentally at odds with a world view in which Nature does what it does, regardless of whether it is observed or not by a human, a cat, or some instrument. So what do we know that Einstein didn’t? For starters, modern quantum field theory and the Standard Model of particle physics. Then there’s also Bell’s theorem that demonstrates that quantum physics is essentially nonlocal, which is to say, the behavior of the system is governed, in part, by constraints that cannot be nailed down to any specific location in space or moment in time. What it means, in practice, is that the state of a quantum system is constrained not just by the past and the present but also by the future, yet the physics remains causal in the sense that rearranging something in the future has no observable consequences on the past (sorry, no quantum time machines). In light of this, the probabilistic interpretation gains a new meaning: ignore the future constraint and the system becomes underdetermined. Instead of telling us what the future will be, the (underdetermined) wavefunction now indeed just yields probabilities. When the future becomes the present, and the outcome of an experiment becomes known, the probability becomes a certainty and we can replace the old wavefunction with a new one (“wavefunction collapse”) in our description of the system. Would this have made Einstein more comfortable? I don’t know. But I do believe that this is markedly different from the quantum physics Einstein knew. Which implies that yes, he was right to criticize quantum mechanics and, in particular, its Copenhagen interpretation. As a local theory, quantum mechanics is necessarily incomplete (again, I am alluding to Bell’s theorem here) and leads to the unsatisfying probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation. But what we got in exchange is, in some ways, even weirder. Yes, quantum field theory has spectacular successes. It can do what quantum mechanics could not ever do, model how particles are created and destroyed. It is also robustly causal and relativistic. But it is just as nonlocal as quantum physics has ever been, and with Bell’s theorem, we know that this nonlocality is not going to go away. Then there’s the problem of renormalizability: We have no renormalizable quantum field theory of gravitation. To many, it seems to imply that the Standard Model (and by extension, quantum field theory as a whole) is just a useful “effective” theory, which will fail at the Planck energy scale, to be replaced by something more fundamental that would unify particle physics with gravity in a more satisfactory way than, say, semiclassical gravity. But much of what I described here happened after Einstein’s death. The quantum theory that he was critical of was really not modern quantum field theory, but quantum particle physics, along with the probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation. I think his criticism of that school of thought was spot on. What was not spot on is his relentless attempt to construct a more fundamental classical theory, which consumed much of his time in the final decades of his life, but ultimately proved futile, little more than a half-forgotten footnote in the history of modern physics. (To anyone seriously interested in the subject, beyond the superb scientific biography of Einstein by Abraham Pais, I’d recommend the hard-to-find 1966 monograph, Einstein’s Unified Field Theory, by Marie-Antoinette Tonnelat.) How is mass not conserved when it's literally E^2-p^2, and both quantities are conserved? The equation, m 2 = ( E / c 2 ) 2 − ( p / c ) 2 , or simpler yet, using units such that c = 1 , m 2 = E 2 − p 2 , indeed describes the invariant rest mass of an isolated particle. However, it does not imply that rest mass is conserved in interactions. As a simple example, consider the collision of an electron and a positron. In the center-of-mass reference frame, their three-dimensional momenta are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction: p e = − p p where I used p to represent the 3-dimensional momentum vector. And of course both the electron and the positron have the same invariant rest mass m e . So before the collision, we have m 2 e = E 2 e − p 2 e , m 2 e = E 2 p − p 2 p , for the respective particles, from which we can also conclude that E e = E p = E (i.e., I dropped the superfluous index), so the total energy of the system is 2 E . The total momentum of the system is, of course p e + p p = 0 according to the rules of vector addition, and the total rest mass 2 m e . The collision annihilates the electron-positron pair, producing (usually) two photons. Energy and momentum are conserved. That means that the momenta of the two photons must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their vector sum is zero. And the total energy of the two photons is 2 E . This implies that each photon has energy E with a corresponding momentum of p = E / c in magnitude, pointing in opposite directions for the two photons. The rest mass, however, is now zero. As an aside, I would like to mention two more thoughts, not directly pertinent to what I just demonstrated, but food for thought, nonetheless. First of all, this reasoning can also inform you right away why an electron-positron pair cannot annihilate into a single photon. In the center-of-mass reference frame, the net momentum must be zero, both before and after; but the energy is nonzero. If the result of the annihilation was a single photon, it would have zero momentum but nonzero energy, which is not possible. Second, now that I demonstrated that the sum of rest masses is not invariant, allow me to offer a twist of the story. Imagine this whole thing took place inside a closed box. Both before and after, the respective particles (the electron-positron pair before the annihilation, the photons after) interact with the walls of the box that keep them confined. Well, guess what: the rest mass of the total system (measured, e.g., by measuring the force that is required to accelerate the box at a certain rate) remains unchanged throughout the process. Which is just a demonstration of the rather important point: namely that the rest mass of a system is equivalent to its internal energy-content. It does not matter what form that energy is in: kinetic energy, potential energy, even the rest masses of constituent bits. The rest mass of the box is the total internal energy of the box material and everything it encloses.

Why is a true “random number generator” impossible? Given the large number of answers already offered to this question (many of which are quite sensible, actually) I hesitate to add my own voice. Still, perhaps it is warranted. That is because I feel compelled to begin my answer with a question myself: What is "random" in this context? What would be the criteria by which we consider a random number generator to be a) “good”, b) "true"? What does "good" mean if I need a random number generator to do a Monte Carlo simulation representing a physics problem? Why, I want the sequence of numbers to be free of any obvious autocorrelation: future numbers should not be trivially predictable from recent numbers. Repetitive patterns are a bad thing, as they can either mask or amplify real physics. For instance, if I were to use a random number generator to simulate a physical system emitting or absorbing radiation, I'd like to be assured that when I see a peak at a specific frequency, it's real physics, not an artifact of a bad random number generator. On the other hand, I don't mind at all if the sequence of "random" numbers is deterministic: Quite the contrary, this is actually Good News, because it allows me to have repeatable numerical experiments! It also allows me to test how sensitive my system is to the random number sequences themselves; e.g., a machine learning neural network may be quite sensitive to how its cells are initialized using different sets of random numbers so I can repeat experiments using different seed values with the same random number generator, to see how the network responds. But then, there is cryptography. There, too, the desire is to have random numbers that are unpredictable, but the "unpredictable" part means something quite different. Autocorrelation may not be of great concern when relatively short sequences are generated (e.g., a 1024-bit random key). But we want to make sure that the result cannot be predicted from related information. Simply using a good random number generator algorithm is not good enough. A hacker might guess which algorithm was used. In fact, if the software is open source, they don't even need to guess. So we need something else: a "truly" random seed value. Something that is not generated by any deterministic algorithm. As these two examples demonstrate, what constitutes a good random number generator depends on the application. In the case of a physics simulation, we are perfectly okay with a deterministic algorithm (in fact, it may be a desirable feature!), so long as the sequence it generates has the desired statistical properties. In the case of a cryptographic application, while statistical goodness is important, it's even more important that the generation of random numbers must be non-deterministic, so that its output cannot be predicted even when all details about the system are available. Modern operating systems offer the best of both worlds. There are algorithms, software libraries for high-quality deterministic random number generation, which can be used effectively in physics, machine learning, etc., problems. There are also options to generate "hardware" random numbers from sources of "randomness" that can include anything from the system clock to user actions to random, unpredictable bits from network traffic or the computer hardware itself. However, collecting enough "entropy" can be time consuming, so hardware random numbers are often used as seed values for a deterministic random number generator, instead of being used directly. It is, of course, also possible to create dedicated hardware generating random noise. What if when your at the singularity of a black hole (if there is one), looking back out to space may look like a singularity also? Can that be? Ok-kay… when you are “at the singularity” of a black hole, your world has come to an end. The singularity is not a place you can be at, but a time: specifically, for anything unfortunate enough to have crossed the event horizon of a (Schwarzschild) black hole, it is an unavoidable moment in time in the near future. In case you are wondering what you might see after you crossed the event horizon but before your world ends at the singularity: no, you cannot “look back”. Not without a time machine. Like the singularity, the event horizon is also a moment in time: a moment in time in your past now. Your present is characterized by an environment that can be mathematically described by the same equations as a collapsing mini-universe. (You may not be a “comoving observer” so the mini-universe might have a skewed appearance, so to speak, but that makes no real difference.) This mini-universe is collapsing and there’s nothing you can do about it, just as there’s nothing you can do, here and now, tou avoid encountering 8 AM tomorrow a few hours from now. So no, you cannot look back. Now whether or not it is even possible to reach an event horizon or if it perhaps evaporates first, or whether or not a black hole with even a small amount of rotation might look materially different “inside” from the Schwarzschild case… I don’t know, and I don’t think anyone has an unambiguous answer, since Hawking evaporation remains a semiclassical model, and as for spinning black holes, no one constructed yet a fully convincing model of what a collapsing, spinning cloud of matter does beyond the horizon. But we do know how things work in the case of a non-spinning Schwarzschild black hole: There is no looking back. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Does a spinning (Kerr) black hole precess about its axis of rotation; if so, relative to what? No, a Kerr black hole does not precess. It is, by definition, an axisymmetric solution of Einstein’s vacuum field equations and as such, no precession is involved. A Kerr black hole in the process of formation may exhibit precession, e.g., as a part of the famous “ringdown” phase of a black hole merger that has been observed by gravitational wave detectors over the course of the past decade. Precession is not relative to anything: acceleration, including acceleration related to rotation or more complex motion like precession, is absolute. Or you could say that acceleration (including rotation and precession) can be measured as deviations relative to a local inertial (non-accelerating) reference frame, but that is a bit tautological. Why does general relativity predict that the wavelength of light will be shifted due to the galaxies mass in an effect called gravitational redshift? Relativity theory predicts two things that can result in redshift: Clocks in a gravitational field tick slower than clocks in empty space. Consider a light source that produces green light at a frequency of 6 trillion cycles a second. Suppose this light source is in a strong gravitational field. You observe it and measure that indeed, the light source produces 6 trillion cycles a second according to a clock right next to it. But then you measure that light using an instrument in deep space. The light appears yellow. You measure it and it's comes in at only 5 trillion cycles per second according to a clock next to your receiver. Even though the two clocks (the one in the deep gravitational well and the one in deep space) are identical, flawless clocks they will tick at different rates. For ever 6 ticks of the clock in deep space, the clock in the gravitational field will tick only 5 times. As that clock counts to 5, the source emits 30 trillion cycles. The clock in deep space will count six times as those 30 trillion cycles arrive. Now the funny business is that the speed of that light will be measured both at the source and at the detector at 300,000 km/s. Fewer cycles means longer wavelength, then. So the same light that appears to leave the source with a wavelength of 500 nm (that is to say, 500 nanometers between emitted cycles) will be measured at 600 nm between cycles at the receiver in deep space. This is gravitational redshift. Now this example assumed that the locations are stationary. What if they aren't? If the distance between the light source and detector decreases, each subsequent cycle will arrive a little sooner as it had less distance to travel. Conversely, if the distance increases, each subsequent cycle takes a tad longer to arrive. So this, too, can change the number of cycles that are received over a unit of time. This is the Doppler frequency shift (redshift if the distance between source and detector is increasing). Perhaps you were thinking about cosmology. Relativity theory also predicts another important thing: In the cosmos, on the largest of scales, matter is not at rest. Things are either flying apart or coming together (that is to say, the matter density of the cosmos is either decreasing or increasing over time). In our cosmos, things appear to be flying apart. When things are flying apart, the distance between them increases over time. So there is a Doppler redshift. But as the density of matter decreases over time, so does its average gravity. So if light traveled for a long, long time it's coming from a distant past when the gravitational field was stronger so clocks were ticking more slowly compared to the present. So there is also a gravitational component to this cosmic redshift. The Doppler part dominates for relatively nearby galaxies; the gravitational part, for very distant stuff. To stress, I am not talking about the individual galaxy's own gravitational field that can cause a small amount of redshift; I am talking about the overall average gravitational field (i.e., the average magnitude, say, of the curvature scalar, to be a tad technical) that changes over time as the matter density of the cosmos decreases. Which is closer to realization, quantum computing, or fusion power? (by "realization" I mean results and mass implementation.) Since I was asked… It might be my ignorance speaking, but I remain immensely skeptical about both. First, let me tell you something about fusion power. Or rather, let me quote a few sentences from a book on my bookshelf. “At the beginning of the 1950s, it seemed that success is not far away. But later, difficulties arose one after another […] To date, more than a hundred different models have been devised […] … When will the first fusion power plants be realized, when will the investigation of controlled nuclear fusion exit the constraints of laboratory experiments? According to Professor Igor Golovin, the world-renowned expert on thermonuclear research, it will be possible to develop Tokamak devices into electricity-producing equipment by the last decade of our century. L. Hirsch, one of the leading physicists of the American Atomic Energy Commission is a little more cautious. According to him the path from the first experiments to the worldwide spread of fusion power plants is longer, and we’re lucky if they will enter the world’s energy production market in fifty years.” I am sure the language sounds familiar. But here is the thing: What I just quoted is text from a book published in 1972. It was titled “Boys’ Almanac, 1973”, published in the Hungarian language (translation mine), a Christmas gift I received from my parents in 1972. Here is the thing about fusion. The only reliable known method of confinement — keeping light atoms hot enough yet close enough to one another to ensure that the undergo fusion at a decent rate — is called gravitational confinement, and requires the weight of an entire star like the Sun. And even deep in the solar interior, fusion remains very inefficient: It produces no more than a few hundred watts of power per cubic meter, which is no ore than what comes out of a well-maintained compost pile. Why is the Sun so hot then? Because it’s big. There are a ginormous number of cubic meters in its interior. That is a luxury we are not afforded here on the surface of the Earth. We don’t have a hundred thousand Earths worth of hydrogen and the room to store it. Rather, for a practical fusion power plant, we’d need something like several hundred megawatts per cubic meter. And we do not have gravitational confinement, so we have to devise all sorts of strange means, lasers, magnetic fields, you name it, to keep the plasma stable. But we also want to remove thermal energy efficiently, in order to use it, e.g., to drive a steam turbine and turn it into electricity. Except that in the case of fusion, temperatures are so high, most of that thermal energy appears in the form of gamma rays. Long story short, despite claimed successes, I remain extremely skeptical that fusion power will ever become useful as a practical, industrial-scale source of electricity. Now on to quantum computing. Don’t let the magical properties of the word, “quantum”, dazzle you. The basic premise is far simpler. It’s about digital vs. analog computing. A digital computer operates, well, on digits: 1, -23, 3.14159265359. An analog computer does not use digits but continuous quantities, such as a length, a voltage, an electric current, to represent quantities. For instance, an analog computer can add two numbers by combining two currents together and then reading off the result from the scale of an ammeter. There are certain mathematical problems that are difficult to solve on a digital computer. A good example is finding the factors of a very large number. Factorizing a 1000-digit number is beyond the capabilities of any digital computer now, or in the foreseeable future. Yet we know that far more efficient factorization algorithms exist for analog computers. The problem is that analog computers are very inaccurate. Try reading the needle of that ammeter with a precision of one part on a thousand. How about one part in a million? Quantum computers are fundamentally like analog computers. A “qubit” may have two “eigenstates” but its actual state is determined by the phase of its wavefunction, which is a continuous, analog quantity. When qubits interact in a quantum computer, it’s these analog quantities that interact. Again, analog computers are imprecise, and quantum computers are no exception. In fact, they are plagued by interactions with the environment (decoherence) which “collapses” qubits to those binary eigenstates. However, there exists an intriguing theorem, the threshold theorem: if a quantum computer can keep its error rate below a certain threshold, there exist error correction methods that allow it to emulate a “perfect” quantum computer. There, you have it. A perfect quantum computer is scalable (more qubits can be added without destroying its perfect-ness) and it can solve certain families of problems in ways digital computers cannot. But is this threshold achievable? Billions of dollars are wagered on that promise. Yet I am skeptical. Moreover, simply achieving the threshold is not enough; the number of qubits for error correction might still be excessive an impractical. So we need to do significantly better. In any case, I suspect (I emphasize: I do not know, this is my personal speculation) that the threshold theorem will be shown to be a “no go” theorem, someone cleverer and I proving through rigorous mathematics that the threshold is not achievable in principle. In any case, the threshold has not been achieved yet. Everything you see about quantum computing, all those claims of successes, “quantum supremacy” and whatnot, are basically side quests: the main quest remains unresolved.

Is there a measurable amount of energy in a gram of mass? Well, yes… but no. Yes, in the sense that mass and energy are equivalent. That is the true meaning of the famous equation everyone knows, E = m c 2 . It’s not about converting anything into anything. Certainly not about converting mass into energy. It simply is the mathematical form of Einstein’s statement that the inertia(l mass) of a body is equal to its energy-content. (The c 2 part is just a conversion factor between incompatible units.) But no, not in the sense of energy as “the ability to do work”, that is, putting things into motion. We extract useful energy from things when we can convert those things into other things with less energy-content. Take a quantity of combustible fuel and the corresponding quantity of oxygen. By allowing combustion to take place, we produce something that is ever so slightly less in mass (i.e., energy-content). The difference is extracted in the form of heat or pressure, which we can use to put things into motion. Or take something at a higher elevation, say, a large quantity of water. We allow it to flow downward, while spinning a turbine. The end result is that the water is now at a lower elevation, This means less gravitational potential energy. The energy extracted was used to bring the turbine into motion. But now take an inert lump of iron? What do you do with it? What’s the lower energy state you can bring it to? Without adding oxygen, you can’t burn it. If it’s not in a gravitational field, it cannot fall. It will not release energy either through nuclear fusion or nuclear fission. So… it’s a dead lump of iron. No “reasonable amount of energy” that can be extracted by any sensible means. (And no, annihilation with antimatter does not count. Someone would have to produce that antimatter in the first place.) So yes, technically, every gram of mass is equivalent to 89875517873681764 ergs of energy. That’s a lot. Comparable to an atom bomb. But in many (most? almost all?) cases, only a tiny fraction of this energy, exists as “energy” in the sense of the ability to do work, i.e., bring things into motion. Light is deflected by gravity. But look at this explanation: Why is there deflection of starlight in the Newtonian model? Shouldn't it simply be straight? https://qrcd.org/5VmM Reply Newtonian gravity would predict a deflection if light if light consisted of particles. Newtonian gravity, however, does not predict a similar deflection if light is described as a wave theory, namely as electromagnetic radiation in Maxwell’s theory. General relativity, in contrast, predicts a deflection in both cases. Moreover, the deflection it predicts is twice the deflection that one would predict using Newtonian gravity. That is because, to get a bit more technical, in addition to the temporal part of the metric tensor (which is what’s behind Newtonian gravity) for anything moving at or near the vacuum speed of light, the spatial part offers an equal contribution, doubling the deflection. This is why the deflection of light was offered as a crucial test of general relativity, and why Eddington’s 1919 solar eclipse expedition, which confirmed Einstein’s prediction, was so important. Could TV interferences be caused by radiation from the Big Bang? First of all, I apologize for being nitpicky, but I see this expression often and I try to offer an important clarification: there is no “radiation from the Big Bang”. There is radiation of cosmological origin, but it was produced roughly 385,000 years after the presumed Big Bang (i.e., the earliest times when matter in the universe was extremely hot and extremely dense). By this time, matter in the universe cooled down, ionized gas recombined into transparent, neutral atoms (mostly hydrogen and helium) and became transparent to its own incandescence. This radiation, redshifted by cosmic expansion, arrives today at a microwave frequency that corresponds to thermal radiation at a temperature of 2.7 K, which is to say, very near absolute zero. That is the “temperature of deep space” if you want to be poetic about it: that is to say, if you left an object floating in deep space far from anything that emits heat or light, the object will cool to this temperature and no further. At this temperature, the object would be in thermal equilibrium with “deep space”, i.e., the cosmic microwave background (CMB). It is an often heard urban legend that on an analog TV set, the “snow” or “static” you see when a channel is not broadcasting is noise from the CMB. This is not really true. A reasonable estimate is that no more than a few percent of the noise picked up by a receiver in the FM or television bands is due to the CMB; the rest is a combination of the thermal noise of the receiver and other (mostly artificial) noise sources that are present in the environment. (For some details, see this StackExchange answer.) And it would not be “interference” in the sense the word is typically used. The CMB contribution is pure thermal noise. At its worst, it would show up as additional “snow” in the screen when an analog receiver picks up a very weak signal, or a slightly worse data rate, slightly higher error rate in case of a digital receiver. Why do electrons have mass, but photons don't? Aren't they both just packets of energy? First of all, particles are not just “packets of energy”. They are “excitations” of the underlying field, but those “excitations” carry more than just energy: they are quantized packets of energy, momentum, angular momentum, and perhaps a variety of charges as well. Depending on the nature of the field it may or may not be a field with “rest mass”. A field is said to have rest mass when it interacts with itself (so even when it’s not interacting with anything else, it has potential energy) or if it interacts with what is called the nonzero vacuum expectation value (v.e.v.) of some other fields (in the actual universe, one such field exists, the Higgs field). In the quantum theory of electromagnetism there are two fields: the electromagnetic field and the field of electrons (or electronic field). These two fields are distinct, but interact with each other. Specifically, the electronic field can serve as a “source” for the electromagnetic field, on account of the fact that its excitations carry electric charge. The electronic field also interacts with the Higgs field v.e.v., so it has potential energy (i.e., its excitations have rest mass-energy) even when it’s not interacting with anything else. Interactions between the electromagnetic field and the electronic field can lead to the creation or annihilation of excitations: photons, or electrons. Conservation laws must always be satisfied, however. So for instance, a lone electron cannot emit a photon; in the electron’s center-of-mass reference frame, the electron has no kinetic energy, so emitting a photon would leave the electron with negative kinetic energy. Conversely, lone electrons cannot be created as that would violate charge conservation; rather, they come in the form of electron-positron pairs. Throughout it all, as I said, each excitation carries these conserved properties. The excitations of the electromagnetic field (photons) and the electronic field (electrons) are manifestly different.
