Can quantum computers, optical computers, new semiconductors, improved energy efficiency, and various other methods make a 10^24flops computer (1 million times faster than today's speed) possible in 30 years? Yes, except for the “quantum computer” bit. If nothing else, massively parallel architectures may produce extreme computing capacity. But quantum computers are not about speed or processing power. They are about doing things differently. Instead of operating on distinct digits, quantum computers internally operate on continuous quantities, namely the phase of the wavefunction in some shape or form. This effectively makes them analog computers, but with a twist: it is possible in principle to introduce error correction that makes a quantum computer capable of emulating an error-free quantum computer. The hard part, however, is that this error correction is possible only if the quantum computer is sufficiently well isolated from its environment, so that the wavefunction governing its behavior is determined entirely by the computer itself, not by the environment. The required level of isolation, or threshold, has not been achieved yet and some (myself included) wonder if it ever will be. If this threshold is not reached, truly scalable quantum computing will not become reality. But let’s suppose my skepticism is misplaced and the threshold theorem is beaten. So we have scalable quantum computers. Does this mean exaflops and such? Certainly not. The point of quantum computers is not speed. It’s their ability to run certain algorithms that have no counterparts on digital computers. That allows a (slow) quantum computer solve certain families of problems that would take an eternity to solve even with the fastest conceivable digital computer. These problems include, e.g., problems in number theory, which would allow a quantum computer, in principle, to break encryption algorithms. Meanwhile, offshoots of quantum computer research show promise in specific areas; e.g., quantum annealing to solve tough optimization problems. But, I stress, such solutions, though valuable in their own right, are not about the core promise of scalable quantum computing. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless? Brian Greene’s “explanation” is one of many popularizations of physics that are intended to make difficult topics accessible to the “unwashed masses” but in reality, achieve the exact opposite. I would put it in the same basket in which I put the “rubber sheet” analogy of gravity, the “expanding balloon” description of cosmic expansion, even the “miniature solar system” models of the atom. Then I would put that basket out onto the curbside for collection. No, particles do not “burrow through” anything. If they “burrowed” through anything, that would mean a loss of kinetic energy through dissipative processes. Soon enough, everything would come to a halt, floating in some sticky molasses I suppose… But no, I swear, that is not how the Higgs works. Remember that mass is energy? No, mass is not “converted” into energy or vice versa. What we call inertial mass, or rest mass, is the internal energy-content of a thing. That’s what E = m c 2 is about, not about nuclear energy or converting anything into anything: It literally tells you that mass and (internal) energy are the same thing. Equivalent. Unsurprisingly, the equation itself is called the mass-energy equivalence relationship. In the Standard Model of particle physics, most particles start off as massless particles, but they interact with the Higgs field. However, the Higgs field has a very peculiar property. In empty space (i.e., the lowest energy state achievable, the vacuum) the Higgs field itself is not “empty”, so to speak. So particles can interact with it even when there’s supposedly nothing there. In effect, particles interact with the vacuum. Interaction means potential energy. (E.g., when two objects interact by, say, repelling one another, you need to invest energy to push them together, and that energy will be “stored” as their interaction energy while they are close to each other.) When an initially massless electron, for instance, interacts with the vacuum, it means it carries that interaction energy with it, no matter what it does or where it goes. And because the vacuum is everywhere, so to speak, the electron cannot get rid of that interaction energy. It’s always there. That interaction energy shows up, for all practical intents and purposes, as part of the energy-content of that electron. And as I stated above, energy-content means inertial mass. So the electron behaves as a massive particle, because no matter where it goes, what it does, it carries along that interaction energy with the vacuum Higgs field (to be more precise, the so-called vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v., of the Higgs field). So I stress, no “burrowing” is involved. The Higgs field has no rest frame, and how fast or how slow the particle moves with respect to this non-existent rest frame is irrelevant. In its own reference frame, a particle is always at rest. But it still has inertial mass, because the potential energy of its interaction with the Higgs field is there, no matter what.

Is it possible that our entire existence is contained within a black hole or space-time singularity without our knowledge of what lies outside of it? No, it is not possible. Spacetime inside a black hole is a collapsing spacetime. To an observer stuck inside the black hole, it would appear quite the opposite to what we actually see in the cosmos: Instead of cosmic expansion, they would see cosmic contraction, with distant objects appearing at ever increasing blueshifts. The universe would be characterized by a future singularity, “the end of time”, characterized by divergent density and gravitational fields, and literally the end of time, geodetic incompleteness. As to the singularity itself, it is (apart from even more pathological versions) a moment in time, not a place, certainly not something you can can be “within”. Can you enter 5 PM next Tuesday and look around? It’s not a place. There is, however, one (speculative) possibility; The cosmos we see could be the interior of a time-reverse black hole, i.e., a white hole. A white hole is characterized by as past singularity (check) and, assuming matter is distributed within it more or less evenly, by the so-called Friedmann equations (check). But this is where spacetime geometry gets really tricky. The sentence “what lies outside of it” kind of suggests that there is a contemporaneous “inside” and “outside”. But that is not the way it works. Just as the event horizon of a black hole (and by extensions, everything within it) lies in the future of any and all observers outside of the black hole, the event horizon of a white hole (and anything within) lies in their past. Conversely, anything “outside” the white hole, from the perspective of someone inside the white hole, is part of the future. It has not happened yet. There is no contemporaneous “outside” where things happen outside our knowledge. Whatever exists outside is yet to happen, and will only happen, by our own reckoning, once we ourselves are “outside”. But the weirdest part perhaps is that we would not even know when that moment happens. Locally, crossing the event horizon is not in any which way special. There is no flash of light, no final message from a divine being to its creation, or any other indication that hey, “NOW” is the moment when you are no longer trapped inside a white hole! That day would look exactly like any other day. Yes, relativity is weird.

Can a massless photon be depicted with kinetic energy since kinetic energy involves mass, yet a photon is massless which diametrically discredits Planck's and Einstein's disjointed theories? Kinetic energy does not necessarily involve mass. For particles that have nonzero rest mass, the expression for kinetic includes their mass. But kinetic energy is a much more general concept, a constant of the motion if you wish, applicable to all systems that are governed by equations that are time translation invariant. And yes, that includes massless photons. In the “disjointed” theory of relativity, of course, time is an observer-dependent concept. Invariance under spacetime translations, however, implies the conservation of a four-dimensional quantity, the so-called four-momentum of the object. Once a specific coordinate system is picked, this four-momentum can be split into an energy term and a three-dimensional conventional momentum term. But this split is, again, observer-dependent. For objects with rest mass, there exists a reference frame in which the object is, well, at rest. In this reference frame, obviously there is no kinetic energy. There is still an energy term, however; it’s the rest mass-energy of the object. In all other reference frames, the energy term is the sum of the rest mass-energy and the kinetic energy of the object. If the object is massless, however, it has no rest mass and no rest frame; the energy term is entirely due to kinetic energy in all reference frames. What is quantum? Which things fit the definition of quantum? There are things that are “quantized”, which is to say, exhibit behavior that comes in distinct chunks, and the branch of physics that deals with these things is called therefore “quantum physics”. But to the extent that it even touches on the concept of “quantum”, it’s a consequence, not a foundation. Not anymore. At first, quantum physics was mostly empirical. Yes, it was based on the idea that atoms emit or absorb energy in such discrete chunks, or quanta. This was observed. This led, for instance, to Planck’s famous radiation law, which marks the dawn of quantum physics. But over time, we became a tad more sophisticated. Less then thirty years after Planck initiated his revolution, the “new” quantum theory of Heisenberg and Schrödinger emerged. It was no longer about atoms emitting and absorbing quanta, but something far more fundamental: the mathematical representation of the state of a physical system. In classical physics, constituent parts of a physical system can be characterized by a) where they are, b) how they move. In other words, their positions and their speed (or momenta). These can be represented by numbers. A position is just a set of coordinates. A velocity is a vector that can be characterized by a set of coordinates. As I said, numbers. Then comes the “new” quantum mechanics, which represents positions and momenta by… well, something else. Matrices in Heisenberg’s case, function operators in Schrödinger’s, but the bottom line is the same: These things are not numbers. Specifically, they do not behave like numbers do under multiplication. Take the momenta p and positions q of a system. In classical physics, we can multiply these numbers together and get a result that does not depend on the order of multiplication: p q = q p , or p q − q p = 0. But this is not how positions and momenta behave in the new quantum physics. They obey instead the relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant and, well, i = √ − 1 . This leads to all sorts of weird consequences, which have been confirmed experimentally. Among other things… well, quanta. Take one of the simplest physical systems, a simple oscillator (the so-called harmonic oscillator). Describe it in terms of these non-commuting variables and you get a weird result: The oscillator cannot have arbitrary energies. Its energy is discretized, going up or down by one unit, or quantum at a time. Electrons in an atom are well described by such oscillators as a mathematical model. So there we have it, the quantized behavior of how atoms emit or absorb energy. But quantum physics in general is not really about quanta. It’s not about chopping things up into small units. That might have been the original inspiration more than a century ago, but it has become something much more nuanced. Planck’s quanta are still there, but as a consequence, not as a building block, of the theory. There are plenty of “quantum” systems that have no quantized behavior. E.g., a free particle can have any energy; nothing “quantized” there. The fundamental statement of the theory is not about quanta; it is about the behavior of those key variables, the positions and momenta of a physical system, and how this behavior is described by the mathematics of noncommuting things, as opposed to the mathematics of simple numbers. Like it or not, that is how Nature behaves, as demonstrated by countless experiments. That said, when we go beyond simple quantum mechanics into the realm of quantum field theory, things change a bit. A field, like the electromagnetic field, can be described as a sum of, well, pure waves really, by way of what is called a Fourier-transform. Each of these pure waves behaves like a harmonic oscillator, which we know how to describe using quantum physics. Each of these harmonic oscillators is characterized by those distinct chunks of energy by which the oscillator’s energy can increase or decrease. In quantum field theory, these distinct chunks of energy (and possibly other conserved properties, like charge or angular momentum) turn out to be none other than the things we’ve know, we’ve observed, as particles! So there you have it: elementary particles come closest to the concept of “quantum”. (Indeed, sometimes we even say so explicitly: e.g., “photons are the quanta of the electromagnetic field.”) If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

I’m having a bit of trouble understanding how to visualize elementary particles as waves but doing the photon/gluon/virtual particle interaction processes. I do not understand why antimatter is visually necessary in field animations. Why? You stumbled upon the most fundamental aspect of quantum physics: You cannot visualize or intuit it. I mean it. No, it’s not some ivory tower mentality telling the lowly masses that they are too dumb. I mean… you see, here is a good example. I am sure you, like almost everyone else, tried GPT or one of its cousins. It is striking just how capable these language models are, yet sometimes, they fail even on relatively simple tasks. Why? Because they cannot visualize anything. They simply lack the hardware, the senses, the training data. GPT can only think in terms of words, not in terms of shapes, diagrams, visuals. We humans can. Why? Because our brain has the hardware. But it’s hardware with limitations. Specifically, the parts of our brain that can do “intuitive” models are capable of modeling a classical, nonrelativistic, three-dimensional universe. Quantum physics does not fit in. It not only cannot be visualized, any attempt to do so actually stands in the way of understanding. Now just like GPT, we can still learn about these things and make inferences. But not by intuiting them. Rather, by using disciplined deductive reasoning, employing the precise language of mathematics. It is hard, of course, just as hard as it is for GPT to reason about the spatial relationships between objects using only the power of words. But it’s the only way. Going back to the subject of the question. The first step is that elementary… .things are neither particles (miniature cannonballs) nor waves in the classical sense. Rather, the mathematical steps basically go like this: We write down the (classical) equations of motion; we do some algebra, re-expressing everything in terms of the state of the system; and then we turn the equation on its head, asking what other states of the system would work. These new solutions make absolutely no sense in the classical world. The electron is neither a miniature cannonball nor a wave: however, it no longer even has a definite position. (Or, if you wish, it’s in many places at once.) Not only that, but the theory is fundamentally nonlocal: Some of the conserved quantities, for instance, that constrain a system cannot be tied to any particular spot in space or time, but constrain the system as a whole. In a quantum particle theory, that electron may interact with an instrument and exhibit classical properties like a specific position: a “particle”. Yet when we describe the state of the system, that state is characterized by a mathematical entity that is a wave solution, a wavefunction, which can be used to compute probabilities of the electron showing up here or there. But the electron is neither that particle-like flash in a detector, nor that wavefunction determining probabilities. The best that we can say is that an electron may exhibit wave-like and particle-like behavior both; but it is neither a wave nor a particle. So what is it, then? To answer that, we need to go beyond a quantum particle theory. But first: a quantum particle theory can also be used to describe a system that is called a harmonic oscillator, well known from classical physics. In quantum physics it acquires a peculiar property: Its energy levels are discrete, “quantized”. This is important. So then, going beyond the particle theory: Meet fields, things that exist everywhere, characterized by values that are assigned to every point in space and every location in time. How can we deal with a field in a quantum theory? Well, we can decompose a field into a sum of harmonic oscillators, a bunch of sine waves. (NOTHING to do with the wavefunction I mentioned above.) Why would we do that? Because each of those harmonic oscillators can be quantized. And now the field’s behavior can be characterized by those harmonic oscillators bumping up or bumping down by one unit of energy at a time. Lo and behold, these can correspond to the creation and annihilation of particles! The equations can get nasty at this point when we try to describe interacting fields. We get some awkward integrals. They can be “tamed” sometimes by expanding them into series and keeping track of ever smaller terms in a summation. Every one of these terms can be conceptualized as an exchange of excitations, i.e., “particles”. They really aren’t particles. But using the concept of a “virtual” particle, which really is just a mathematical tool, we can keep track of these terms. Keep this in mind. Virtual particles are not visualization tools. They are bookkeeping tools, keeping track of terms in a mathematical sum. As to why antimatter is needed, that depends on the specifics of the field involved. Some fields describe particles and corresponding antiparticles. Other fields describe only one type of particle that may serve as its own antiparticle in interactions. In any case, it’s not about any “visual” necessity. It’s simply the nature of the solution, the nature of the theory, whether antiparticles are predicted by it or not. Ultimately of course the theory must agree with experiment. Electrons have antiparticles; photons don’t (they’re their own antiparticles, in a manner of speaking). The theory accurately reflects the nature of both. OK, this answer became longer than I anticipated, so here’s the most important take-home lesson: Do not try to intuit or visualize the quantum world. Any attempt to do so creates an obstacle to understanding. If you seek real, in-depth understanding, unfortunately the math cannot, must not, be avoided as it is the only tool that the human brain has at its disposal to understand something this far removed from our sensory experience. Why doesn’t the Higgs field impart mass to a stationary photon? Is it theHiggs field that gives the photon mass while it is moving? The answer is… a tad complicated. The Higgs field imparts mass on certain particles indirectly through two distinct mechanisms, both of which are linked to a fundamental property of the Higgs field: Its self-interaction potential. Without going into details, for most fields, the lowest-energy state is when the field is free of excitations. For instance, the electromagnetic field is in its lowest-energy state when there are no photons (which are the excitation quanta of the electromagnetic field). Not the Higgs field. Its lowest energy state is when some excitations are present. This is what is expressed through the famous “Mexican hat” potential that are sometimes shown in popular science publications. What this means in practice is that the “vacuum” in which the Higgs field is free of excitations is not really the vacuum: It can decay into a lower-energy state, in which the Higgs field has some excitations. This lowest energy state is what we know as the vacuum. This has two consequences. First, the Higgs field interacts with certain particles (charged fermions) directly. This means that in this new, lowest-energy vacuum, the nonzero excitations (nonzero vacuum expectation value, or v.e.v.) of the Higgs field interacts with those fermions (electrons, quarks, etc.) An interaction means energy, energy means mass… so those fermions, which were initially massless in the theory, now behave as though they had mass all along, carrying this interaction mass-energy as their rest mass. There is another class of particles, vector bosons, which mediate what is known as the “electroweak” force: a unification of the electromagnetic and weak forces. There are four such vector bosons, and they form a particular symmetry group that combines three of the four, while the remaining one has its own, different symmetry group. When the Higgs field leads us to that new, lower-energy vacuum state that I described earlier, the symmetry group of the three vector bosons gets broken. In practice, this manifests itself in the form of interactions that, again, show up as rest mass-energy for these three vector bosons (these are the bosons of what we know as the weak interaction, namely the Z, W+ and W- bosons). However, the photon is unaffected by this symmetry breaking. Higgs or no Higgs, it remains massless, because its unique symmetry group is different in nature, and not sensitive to the Higgs-induced symmetry breaking (it’s a so-called Abelian group). As I said… the answer is a tad complicated. I hope it’s not completely incomprehensible, though.

What happens to an object that falls into a singularity? Does it turn into Hawking radiation or get crushed by gravity? Okay, first of all, Hawking radiation is not about the singularity. It is about the collapsing matter that, in the far future, is supposed to form an event horizon that will hide a singularity (i.e., a moment in time even farther in the future of infalling objects, when they will cease to exist). Now there is a bit of a contradiction here, no doubt a reflection of the fact that the theory is incomplete, that Hawking radiation itself is a prediction of the “bastard child” of classical relativity and quantum field theory, called semiclassical gravity. But if we take the predictions literally… The event horizon is in the infinite future of any and all outside observers. In other words, when you follow infalling matter, no matter how long you wait, the process is reversible in principle; e.g., if one of the infalling “particles” happens to be an astronaut with an amazingly powerful rocket, he may turn around a year, a trillion years, 10 100 years from now and re-emerge, only seconds older as measured by his own clock. You can never be sure if he entered the horizon because no matter how long you wait, that moment remains in the future. This is at least what classical gravity theory predicts. But add quantum field theory, and we end up with Hawking radiation that results in the evaporation of the entire mass of the collapsing object in the form of thermal radiation in finite time. In other words, as seen by outside observers, all the collapsing mass (including our astronaut!) turns into Hawking radiation before the horizon can form. In this picture, our infalling astronaut would also encounter that Hawking radiation but at an accelerated rate as he approaches the (yet-to-form) horizon. The closer he gets to that horizon (which has not yet formed!) the more matter is lost, so the radius of the future horizon continues to shrink, eluding him. Even though he doesn’t reach the horizon, our astronaut is exposed to ever stronger tidal forces, and if he’s foolish enough not to put his rocket to use in time, he is eventually ripped apart by the famed “spaghettification” so yes, my bet would be that he turns into Hawking radiation without ever encountering the horizon, because the horizon ultimately never forms. But I am speculating. Informed speculation perhaps, but as I mentioned, ultimately we’re down to the dilemma caused by combining two theories that are not fully compatible: quantum field theory and a theory of gravity that stubbornly resists quantization (at least the “canonical” way).

Why does the weakness of gravity prevent scientists from finding the graviton? We detect particles by detecting their interactions with other particles. The strength (or weakness) of the coupling between the particles determines the “cross-section”, basically the likelihood, that a detectable interaction occurs. When the coupling is really, really weak, such interactions occur very rarely. In a 2012 lecture[1], the late Freeman Dyson presented an interesting calculation. The Sun, on account of being hot, emits not only thermal electromagnetic radiation but also thermal gravitational radiation. The same blackbody spectrum, just gravitons, not photons. Sure, gravity is very weak compared to electromagnetism, so instead of the several hundred septillion watts that it emits in the electromagnetic spectrum, the Sun “only” emits about 79 megawatts of thermal gravitational radiation, but that is still a respectable radiating power. If we had a 79 megawatt light bulb at 1 astronomical unit (the Sun-Earth distance) from here, we’d have no trouble detecting it, and no trouble detecting individual photon events from that source using a suitable detector. But this 79 megawatts is not in the form of electromagnetic waves but in the form of gravitational waves. Now Dyson imagined using the entire Earth, every last bit of it, as kind of a “perfect” graviton detector: That is, he assumed that we can somehow monitor the entire Earth in a completely noise-free setting, and detect a single atomic transition (an electron jumping to a higher orbit) as a result of capturing a graviton. I.e., direct detection of a graviton, much the same way we can detect photons with a suitable detector. The result: Dyson’s calculation told us that we would see, on average, one such graviton event every billion years or so. That is what it means to have a very weak coupling between the gravitational field and matter. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why is the concept of "gravity slowing down time" used instead of "time moving more slowly near massive bodies"? I was prepared to write an answer questioning if there is even a difference between the two statements but, well, there is. It would have been wrong for me to dismiss this question as silly. It isn’t. Yes, clocks tick more slowly in a gravitational field than elsewhere. This is part of relativity theory: it relates reference frames that may be moving relative to each other (special relativity) or may be in different gravitational fields (general relativity). Yes, massive bodies are a source of gravitation. But the statement I just made about clocks does not care about sources. It does not matter what the origin of that gravitational field is, or how close we are to its source. The field itself has physical existence: it carries energy and momentum, it carries information, it is, in a very literal, physics sense, a thing in ways neither space nor time are things, for instance. And clocks tick more slowly when in a gravitational field. The clock does not know what the origin of that field is. Is there a massive body nearby? Is this a passing gravitational wave? Is it a gravitational anomaly of cosmological origin? Doesn’t matter. The stronger the field, the slower the clock. This is well-reflected by the first statement but not the second, which implies that a) a massive body must always be present nearby (not true) and that b) a massive body directly influences the clock (also not true, the influence is mediated by the gravitational field, it’s due not some “action-at-a-distance” by the massive body). Can time exist without the Higgs field? Rather than trying to answer the question directly (what does it even mean for time to “exist”?) allow me to respond instead by enumerating what exists in the Standard Model of particle physics courtesy of the Higgs field. Courtesy of the Higgs field, we have massive vector bosons. As a result, only one vector boson (the photon) “survives” as a mediator of a long-range interaction (electromagnetism); interactions due to the rest, collectively labeled the “weak force”, become extremely short range, playing only a relatively marginal role in nuclear physics. Courtesy of the Higgs field, we also have charged fermions with masses. In the Standard Model, charged leptons (like the electron) and quarks start their existence as massless particles. But because of their interactions with the Higgs field’s so-called vacuum expectation value, they behave as though they were particles with nonzero rest mass, which allows, among other things, for them to form structures, including protons, neutrons, and ultimately, atoms. So without the Higgs field, we’d have no periodic table, no atoms, no matter as we know it. But “time”? All this takes place on the stage of spacetime. Particle physics exists in spacetime, with or without a Higgs field. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If you were sufficiently close to two colliding black holes, would distortions in space caused by the gravity waves be fatal (ignoring all of the other fatal phenomena like the accretion disk and tidal effects)? Well, technically yes, but by that time you are too close already and you’d be killed by those tides even in the absence of a collision and the resulting gravitational waves. [Pedantic note, with apologies: A “gravity wave” is what you see on the surface of the sea when it waves. A “gravitational wave” is a propagating change in the gravitational field away from sources.] The point is, gravitational waves are propagating changes. A single object produces a gravitational field that changes from place to place but it does not change over time in the inertial reference frame in which the object is at rest. But when we have two objects inspiraling towards each other, no such inertial frame exists. The gravitational field changes not just from place to place but also over time. These changes then ripple away towards infinity with ever decreasing amplitude, much like changes in the electromagnetic field do in response to electric charges undergoing accelerating motion. When the gravitational force changes from place to place, it represents a tidal force. Different parts of a body want to head in different directions or different rates. This can rip a body apart. There are tides near any gravitating object, and tides near a black hole can be very strong because we can get very close to a black hole (they are very compact). When the black holes inspiral, these tidal forces change. Those changes propagate. But they do not get stronger with distance, quite the contrary. And in the end, what kills us is not how the tidal forces change over time, but how strong they are in the first place. Get close enough to the black hole and you’ll find out! A little farther away, though… I once calculated that if you were about the same distance from the merger of two ~30 solar mass black holes as the Earth is from the Sun, you could actually hear the result as a loud rising then decaying sound. Yes, there can be sounds in space! Well, not exactly sounds as we know them, not a traveling longitudinal pressure wave in a medium, rather, transversal gravitational waves in the vacuum but in the end how they travel is not relevant; what is relevant is that at that distance, they are powerful enough to interact with our ears. How do quarks give rise to the mass of protons and neutrons? As you know, the inertial rest mass of a thing is determined by its internal energy-content. This applies to everything: planets, humans, protons and neutrons. So how does this work considering that baryons (protons and neutrons) are made of triplets of quarks? First, the quarks have rest mass. (This rest mass it itself a result of an interaction between the quarks and the so-called vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field.) The rest masses of the constituent quarks about to roughly 1% of the rest masses of protons and neutrons. As for the rest, it’s the binding energy between those quarks. Think of the strong interaction (very crudely) as a force that’s like a tension spring. The tension spring is relaxed when it’s at its shortest. That’s when it has zero potential energy. When you stretch it, you invest work, add energy to the system. So think of those three quarks as being connected by tension springs. OK, things get a tad more complicated than that. First of all, a lot (and I mean a lot!) of energy is added to the system this way, so that means that as the springs do their thing, those quarks can start zipping around at high speed (though still safely inside the baryons). So a lot of the energy invested into the system is in the form of the kinetic energy of the quarks, not de facto tension in the springs themselves. Moreover, the tension in these springs is such that they can “snap”: in the case of the quark model, that means producing new ends for the spring fragments, which is to say, new quark-antiquark pairs. But these configurations are unstable, so the springs reconnect quickly, the quark-antiquark pairs vanish as quickly as they appear. The result is a soup, a continuous balance between potential energy, kinetic energy, virtual quark-antiquark pairs… but ultimately, as I said, it’s the binding energy between the three constituent quarks, whatever form it takes at any specific moment, that yields roughly 99% of the inertial rest mass of a proton or neutron. How does Einstein's equation demonstrate the conversion of matter into energy? Can this process be reversed to create more matter than needed? It does not. The famous equation, E = m c 2 (which is not really called Einstein’s equation, but let me put pedantry aside for a moment) is absolutely NOT about any conversion of “matter” into energy. To explain what this equation IS about, first allow me to recall the title of the paper in which this equation (in a slightly modified form) is introduced: “Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content?” (Ist die Trägheit eines Körpers von seinem Energiegehalt abhängig? Annalen der Physik. 18:639, 1905.) The question is answered by the paper in the affirmative, establishing something important: that what we know as the inertia, i.e., the mass (its resistance to acceleration) of a body is, in fact, its energy-content. You add energy to a body (e.g., making it warmer), its inertia increases. You remove energy from a body, its inertia decreases. Notably, the equation is not about converting anything into anything. It is, in fact, called the mass-energy equivalence relation. Which is to say, it expresses recognition of the fact that a body’s mass (its inertia, resistance to acceleration) and its intrinsic energy-content (not to be confused with energy that exists relative to other reference frames, such as the body’s kinetic energy in a moving observer’s reference frame) are really equivalent: they are the same thing. Now about that pedantry bit: The expression, “Einstein’s equation”, is usually used to refer to the equation R μ ν − 1 2 g μ ν R = 8 π G T μ ν , which is Einstein’s (field) equation for gravitation, i.e., the fundamental equation of general relativity. Note that all along, I’ve been silent about the word “matter”. This concept is not even defined in relativity theory. The contribution of matter to the field equations is characterized by the stress-energy-momentum tensor T μ ν , but the theory remains silent about what “matter” really is. This is also true when it comes to E = m c 2 . Presumably a “body” would be made of “matter”, but again, the theory remains silent as to its nature. It only talks about its specific, measurable properties, namely its resistance to acceleration (mass) and changes in its energy-content. The closest thing to “creating” matter happens in particle accelerator experiments, when lighter particles collide with plenty of excess kinetic energy as measured in the reference frame of their common center-of-mass. The collision converts them into new particles, which may be heavier than the progenitors, which is to say that some of that kinetic energy of the collision now becomes the internal energy-content of the collision products. These products are usually short-lived, unstable particles however, so very quickly they decay back into lighter particles, with some (most?) of their energy-content now turning back into the kinetic energy of these decay products. But other than the fact that all along the process, mass-energy is conserved, the equation E = m c 2 has nothing to do with such processes of particle creation and annihilation. Was Heisenberg the first one to promote the use of tensors in physics? No, it was not Heisenberg. Let me show you a snapshot from a page from an interesting paper: Sure, the notation is a bit archaic, but what you are looking at is the Cauchy stress tensor, which characterizes the stresses and pressures in a medium. This snapshot is from a later reprint of Cauchy’s 1827 paper, De la pression ou tension dans un corps solide [Ex. Math. 2 (1827) p. 42]. So as you can see, tensors were already in use in mathematical physics two centuries ago. Later, in the early 20th century, tensors became the essential tool for relativity theory, especially general relativity. The reason is that the tensor concept perfectly captures the difference between the geometric object (which exists independently of any choice of coordinates) vs. its representation in a specific coordinate system. The independence of physics from the coordinates used to represent it is a fundamental concept in relativity theory (and, well, modern physics in general). Heisenberg, incidentally, did not use tensors much to my knowledge. His matrix mechanics was something else: it was a means to represent the observables of quantum physics, for instance, positions and momenta that do not behave like the ordinary numbers of classical physics, specifically they do not commute under multiplication. Later it was shown that Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics was mathematically equivalent to representing the same quantities using function operators acting on Schrödinger’s wavefunction. But those matrices were not used to represent tensor quantities. However, tensors entered the world of quantum physics with a vengeance, starting with the 1930s, with the development of quantum field theory. Mass and energy are equivalent. Heavy masses dilate time. Could enough energy in a closed container dilate time? If not, why not? I have a feeling reading this question that it was inspired by some kind of (unfortunately fairly common) magical misunderstanding of “energy”. What do you think “energy” is? Is it something that we can scoop out of a container with a ladle? Use it to fill another container to the brim? Not really. By and large, energy can be two things: Potential energy or kinetic energy. Potential energy is associated with how things interact with each other, attracting or repulsing one another. This is the ability to do work: The ability to bring things into motion. Kinetic energy, in turn, is the energy associated with the motion itself. So then, going back to the question: To put “energy” in the box, we need to put things into the box: things that interact (with each other or even with themselves), things that move. And all these things will add to the energy-content of the box. As per the mass-energy equivalence relationship, it means that the box will have more inertia. More mass, in other words. and yes, that also means more gravity. But then, let me get to the second part of the question. Heavy masses dilate time? Not exactly. I know, we say that, I probably said that a few times, lazy language and all, but let’s keep in mind that the theory is called the theory of relativity for a reason: it’s not about what happens to time, it’s about what, for instance, two clocks measure that follow different worldlines between the same two events. I.e., how the two clocks behave relative to one another. And yes, by and large, clocks that spend more time in a gravitational field tend to count fewer ticks, but that’s because their worldlines are, in an abstract sense, “shorter”, not because of anything that might have happened either to the clocks or to time itself. So yes, a heavy box with plenty of energy-content will have more gravity, and as a result, clocks following worldlines that pass near the box may count fewer ticks. As to why that box is heavy, it doesn’t matter. Heavy always means more energy-content. Whether that energy content exists because we put lead in the box, or because we lined the inside of the box with perfect mirrors and then let in a tremendous quantity of light, never to escape… no difference. What matters, as I said, is the energy-content. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

If blackholes get large enough can they supernova? Nope. It’s the other way around. If a star gets large enough, it may collapse under its own weight, producing a “core collapse supernova” (also known as a Type II supernova). The remnants of that collapse may form a neutron star or, if the progenitor star was massive enough, a black hole. So if the formation of a supernova is the fire, the black hole would be part of the ashes that remain. Ashes don’t catch fire. (This is meant metaphorically, of course.) A black hole may grow over time if more stuff falls into it. Catastrophic events may happen as matter falls into a large black hole, heated to extreme temperatures during the inspiral, for instance. But the black hole itself will not explode, ever. What black holes will do, over absolutely enormous timescales (60, 70, or more digits in the number of years required) is to evaporate by way of Hawking radiation. Because this takes an enormously long time, the intensity of Hawking radiation is exceedingly tiny. Until the very end, that is; because somewhat paradoxically, the smaller a black hole, the more intensely it radiates! To illustrate, when an evaporating black hole has only a day left of its very long life, it still weighs over 12,000 metric tons. That mass is very, very small compared to the mass of a star: by this time, the black hole is almost completely gone. It is still a staggering amount of mass-energy by human standards, though, all of which will be radiated awway in a day. The black hole at this point has a temperature of around 10 quadrillion kelvins, while its size if a tiny fraction of the size of a proton. Even though it is that small, it is putting out over two million terawatts of power, mostly in the form of extreme gamma rays. You really don’t want to be near such a thing. Yet compared to a supernova, it might as well be just light from a failing candle, a tiny spark. Supernovas are so much more powerful. So no, black holes don’t turn into supernovas. Supernovas leave behind black holes. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Does energy have a gravitational field like matter? E.g., has a charged cell battery higher field compared with an empty one of similar mass? Very much so. In fact, It is energy that is the source of gravitation. Remember the famous (and often colossally misunderstood) equation, E = m c 2 ? Its proper name is mass-energy equivalence relation. To clarify, allow me to quote the title of Einstein’s 1905 paper that introduces this relationship: “Does the inertia of a body depend upon its energy-content?” The answer given by the paper is in the affirmative, but the title itself should tell you what you need to know: What we know as a body’s inertia, i.e., its rest mass, is, in fact, its energy-content. The equation E = m c 2 is not about converting anything into anything. It is simply the statement that what we measure as the energy-content of a body, E , can also be measured as its resistance to motion, m , the two measurements being related by the conversion factor c 2 . That conversion factor exists only for cultural reasons, because we humans have chosen incompatible units to measure mass and energy, or ultimately, distance and time. We do so for convenience. But in so-called “natural” units, c = 1 and the mass-energy equivalence relationship is simply E = m . When it comes to gravitation, the source of gravitation is not “matter” (however we define it): It is the energy-content (more precisely, the so-called stress-energy-momentum tensor, but for ordinary matter, that tensor’s only dominant component is the body’s energy-content). This is the mathematics behind the concept of the weak equivalence principle: The gravitational interaction does not care what a body is made of, only its energy-content matters. What form that energy takes is irrelevant. So what happens when you charge a battery? You increase that body’s energy-content. So yes, its inertia changes and by extension, since the gravitational field of a body is sourced by the same inertial mass, its gravitational field changes as well. The change is minuscule. The amount of electrical mass-energy you pump into a battery when charging it is typically a small fraction of a trillionth of the mass of the battery itself, far too small to be measurable. But it’s there. And it should come as no surprise. After all, even for the discharged battery, the bulk of its rest mass is, well, energy! That is to say, almost all the mass of an ordinary object is due to the masses of its constituent baryons (protons and neutrons). Those baryons are made of quarks, but the quarks contribute roughly 1% of their mass. The remaining 99% is the strong force binding energy that holds those quarks together in those protons and neutrons. So next time you lift a heavy object such as a brick, consider: the resistance you feel when you lift it up is almost entirely due to the energy-content of the strong force that ties its subatomic constituents together on microscopic scales, reacting to the Earth’s gravity. Has there been a mistake or intentional deception in the announcement of the discovery of the Higgs particle? No, there is neither a mistake nor any signs of a deception. We’re talking about a discovery that was made over 12 years ago, and has been subjected to plenty of scrutiny since. A plot like this from the CMS experiment tells the story: What it tells us is that there is a slight bump at a specific energy level (approximately 125 GeV) in what appear to be the detections of correlated pairs of photons, and that this bump is consistent with what we would predict if we had a Higgs boson with a rest mass-energy of 125 GeV, decaying into a pair of photons. This is how particle physics experiments are made. Most subatomic particles are not detected directly, because they decay rapidly. However, we know what their decay products are supposed to be, and we can compare that against experiment. Before its discovery, we did not know the mass of the Higgs boson, and while certain mass ranges were excluded, estimates ranged wildly. However, once this bump was detected, things changed. The bump is not particularly significant visually, but it is very significant statistically. Of course just because there’s a bump, we cannot be certain if it is a bump due to the Higgs boson or perhaps something else. So refined experiments look at more specific properties and correlations. For instance, was the detected particle a true scalar (like the Higgs) or perhaps a composite particle that behaves like a so-called pseudoscalar? There were additional experiments that could distinguish between the two. Other hypotheses were also discarded. So now, 12 years later, I don’t think there’s any reason to doubt the validity of this discovery, any more than we might doubt, say, the discovery of the Z boson or the top quark. One question that may not be fully settled yet is whether or not the simplest, minimalist Higgs model is the valid model, or perhaps something more complicated. It would be interesting to see if we could detect a “triple Higgs” interaction, which is a Higgs boson splitting into two Higgs bosons (or equivalently, a Higgs boson emitting or absorbing another Higgs boson).

As Per quantum physics, can a machine collapse a wavefunction (as in a double slit experiment), or must a human actually observe the results, even if indirectly, for the wavefunction to collapse? My real question was longer but exceeded length limit. To offer a somewhat precise answer: Apart from somewhat fringe interpretations of quantum mechanics (“objective collapse”) the “collapse of the wavefunction” is widely regarded as a mathematical abstraction, not a physical process. Indeed, when you think about it, it would be far worse a cure than the problem it is intended to solve. Quantum physics is nonlocal. We have known that for a very long time, and proof exists in the form of Bell’s inequality and similar derivations. This is hard to digest, since it basically means that, for instance, the (unobservable) phase of the wavefunction at present may be constrained by the quantum system’s interaction with an instrument in the future. What if it isn’t? What if the wavefunction actually collapses at the moment the interaction occurs? Well… think about what that means. It means that we take the wavefunction (which describes the state of the system), yank it, and replace it with another wavefunction… in a relativistic quantum theory, we replace one wavefunction with another in the whole of spacetime, everywhere, everytime, future, present and past included. Basically we throw one universe away and replace it with a different one. Meh. I much rather just live with quantum nonlocality. But as for what causes the problem in the first place, well, it is an interaction with a classical system. Interaction with something that is described using classical (non-quantum) equations of motion, in other words. In physical reality, no such systems exist, but many systems behave in such a way that their behavior is indistinguishable from the classical. And no, they need not be humans. They don’t even have to be machines. A rock, a brick, a planet, a cloud of gas, you name it… if its behavior is classical and a quantum system interacts with it, the quantum system’s wavefunction will be constrained by that interaction. No conscious observer required. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why has the cosmic microwave background not been considered to predate time itself, and is therefore infinite? The cosmic microwave background has nothing to do with predating time. It has to do with a specific epoch in an expanding and cooling cosmos, when the bulk matter in the cosmos (mostly hydrogen and helium) was becoming just cold enough to turn from an ionized gas into a gas of electrically neutral atoms. The radiation we see is thermal radiation (incandescence) from this hot gas, emitted everywhere, at that epoch, now capable of traveling freely in all directions. This radiation was emitted when the gas was roughly 3000 K in temperature. The cosmos has continued to expand since then. As a result the wavelength of this radiation has stretched by a factor greater than a thousand, resulting in today’s measurement of 2.7 K as the temperature associated with the radiation (now detected in the form of radio waves). But, I stress, all we are looking at here is opaque, hot, incandescent gas. Looking in the same direction tomorrow, the volume of gas we saw today is now transparent; the light we see tomorrow is light emitted slightly earlier by a slightly more distant volume of gas. That’s why the CMB never stops: Behind every volume of gas we see in a given day in a given direction, there’s more gas behind it, from which light takes a little longer to arrive. Regarding ‘flat’ or ‘curved’ space. How can we measure angles of a triangle with vertices here on earth and at two remote stars to see if they add to 180°? Local angle is easy. I can’t see how to measure the other two as they are remote. Our knowledge that the universe has negligible spatial curvature does not come from direct measurements over astronomical scales. As the question suggests, it really is not possible to directly measure the angles of a triangle of interstellar size. Rather, we look at indirect evidence. Whether it is planetary orbits in the solar system, the large-scale structure of the universe characterized by matter density at various scales, supernova redshift-luminosity data or, importantly, the specific angular spectrum of the cosmic microwave background, these results are consistent only with a universe that has no significant spatial curvature. Can it still have some spatial curvature? Sure. But then we run into something else. The measure of spatial curvature increases over time. So if it is small today, it would have had to be astonishingly small in the distant past. How likely is it that the early universe had a density that was not precisely the critical density, but the critical density plus or minus a tiny, tiny, tiny number, say, 10^{-100}? We’re not talking about measurement error here, but rather, an initial, nonzero but very tiny deviation from the number 1. Yes, it is possible, but it is generally considered very unlikely. Having said that, like in the case of all quantities that are presumed to be small, observations can provide upper limits; we can never say for certain that the quantity does not exist. Other examples include the photon mass (theory suggests that it is zero; measurements tell us that it can at most be some very tiny number, but we can never exclude in principle that the tiny number is not zero), or the range parameter of gravitation (i.e., the mass of the graviton). So perhaps there is a tiny spatial curvature present. Can Hawking radiation (absorption of mass by a hypothetical particle and destruction of mass by a star) occur in a neutron star? Is it possible or not and why? The answer is yes, and I can explain why both using simple reasoning and the math. On the simple reasoning side: If a black hole radiates Hawking radiation in the present, it cannot be because it’s a black hole as the black hole has not formed yet. The particles collapsing into a black hole take forever (as seen by outside observers) to reach the limit when they’d form an event horizon. This is the essence, e.g., of the famous Oppenheimer-Snyder paper that, in 1939, described for the first time this process of “continued contraction”. This also means that, at least in principle, the particles may interact with one another in the last minute, second, picosecond before forming a horizon (as measured in their own reference frame) and turn around; we can never be 100% certain that this won’t happen as the black hole has not formed yet! So perhaps it never will… yet there is Hawking radiation. But never mind the fairy tale. I hold in my hand a paper, well, a single sheet of paper really as Hawking’s paper really is short: It’s his 1974 publication in Nature, titled “Black hole explosions?” Let me quote two key sentences from this paper: “The β i j will not be zero because the time dependence of the metric during the collapse will cause a certain amount of mixing of positive and negative frequencies. […] The number of particles created and emitted to infinity in a gravitational collapse can therefore be determined by calculating the coefficients β i j . ” In short: What is needed for Hawking-radiation is not a horizon but a time asymmetry; specifically, the asymmetry due to collapse, as a result of which the past and the future are not identical. What this tells us is that any collapsing cloud of matter will emit Hawking radiation unless the collapse is halted by some interaction and the configuration becomes static. In the case of a black hole, the collapse never ends. In other cases, it may. But so long as the collapse is in-progress, Hawking radiation follows, according to Hawking’s own reasoning. What does "non-local literally mean? Why is it important? How did Bell's theorem prove it? Bell’s theorem offers insight into how quantum nonlocality works by looking at how distant events in quantum physics are correlated in ways that cannot happen in the classical world. But first, allow me to offer the “classic” classical example: socks. Suppose you travel. You pack your favorite pair of socks. Upon arrival in your hotel room in a distant land, you unpack and realize that only half the pair is present in your suitcase. You instantly gain knowledge that the other half is back at home, thousands of miles away, in your socks drawer. No magic here, of course. Although you only just observed it, the information was there all along. It was in the form of a “local” (carried with you all along) “hidden” (in your suitcase) variable. So now let’s take a look at a quantum physics experiment. We send two particles (say, two electrons) in different directions. The electrons are correlated: their total angular momentum is zero. We then measure both electrons at their respective arrival locations. If the spin of one of them is “up”, the other will be “down”, as expected. Conservation laws are, after all, strict and absolute. So far so good, this is just like the aforementioned socks. But now we introduce a twist. We now change the orientation of one of the measurement devices a little. The two receiving locations are no longer parallel, so we do not expect perfect correlation. But we do expect some correlation. Quantum physics predicts a correlation between the two locations that is just “too good” in a sense. It cannot be explained by classical physics, by local hidden variables. The electron at one of the locations somehow “knows” what the electron at the other location is doing, despite the distance between them, despite the fact that it’s not even clear which electron is measured first, as that depends on who is looking (i.e., the relativistic reference frame in which we describe the experiment). This is the essence of the mathematical statement that is known as Bell’s inequality. Conservation laws in quantum physics are generally like this. You cannot nail them down to any particular location or moment in time, but when you look at a quantum system that is isolated from its environment, it always obeys conservation laws exactly (no probabilities here, conservation laws are exact). Is there any way, other than throwing some mass in the opposite direction, to move forward in space? To move forward in space, you don’t need to do anything. Once a body is in motion, it remains in motion unless a force acts upon it… and in space, no such forces are usually present. However, if you want to accelerate a body, things change. Acceleration means a change in the body’s momentum. But momentum is one of those quantities that are always strictly conserved. So if you change the momentum of a body, the momentum of something else, somewhere, must change by an equal but opposite amount. Reaction mass could be that something else. This is how rockets work. However, if you find something outside of your space vehicle, perhaps you can change its momentum without throwing anything away. For instance, here in the vicinity of the Earth, you might be able to interact with the Earth’s magnetic field and accelerate; in exchange, the Earth itself would accelerate in the opposite direction, but given how much more massive the Earth is compared to a spaceship, this change in the Earth’s momentum is imperceptible. It might be possible to repeat the feat on larger scales, using, e.g., the magnetic field of the Sun or even galactic magnetic fields, albeit these fields are very weak so the sheer size of whatever equipment might accomplish this miracle likely makes the concept impractical. It is also possible to make use of the momentum of something already there, e.g., sunlight. Or the momentum of something we put there ourselves, e.g., light from a powerful ground-based laser. In both cases, the spacecraft would have a lightsail that, as it interacts with (and changes the momentum of) the light it receives, imparts a momentum on the spaceship that carries it. There is also gravitational assist: When there are at least two bodies in a system (and there are certainly more than two bodies here in the solar system) it is possible to follow a trajectory that changes direction with respect to one of the bodies, but changes direction and magnitude of velocity with respect to the other. Again, momentum is conserved: the motion of the bodies involved also changes. But again, bodies such as planets in the solar system are so much heavier than a spaceship, any change in their momenta will remain imperceptible. Throughout it all, however, the common theme is that books must always remain balanced when it comes to momentum. If your spaceship accelerates in some direction, something else — propulsion mass, a planet, rays of light, whatever — must accelerate in the opposite direction. Spacetime is curved by gravity. Can other fields also curve spacetime? Er, no. Spacetime is not curved by gravity. Don’t think of it that way. Rather, gravity is characterized by what is known as a tensor quantity. This tensor quantity “couples to matter universally and minimally”. These two words have specific meaning. “Universally” means that material properties make no difference: gravity couples to matter the same way, regardless of what that matter is made of. “Minimally” means that the coupling is geometric in nature: That is to say, it determines things like inner products between vectors, volume elements in integrals, etc. Putting the two together implies that gravity can be interpreted as a universal geometry, i.e., the geometry of spacetime. Do we have to interpret gravity this way? No, we don’t, and indeed, none other than Einstein himself warned against taking the geometric interpretation too literally. (There are at least two practical reasons: First, taking the geometric interpretation dogmatically prevents us from thinking about alternative theories that do not have these two properties; second, most sensible approaches toward a quantum theory of gravity start with treating gravity as a force, not as geometry.) Can other fields be like gravity? We can certainly contemplate other possibilities. But no other known field has these properties. Electromagnetism couples to charges, so the coupling depends on material properties, such as the charge-to-mass ratio, so it’s not universal, albeit it can be viewed as geometric (indeed, there were early attempts to lump together electromagnetism and gravity by way of geometry: Weyl’s linear vs. quadratic ground forms, or the five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein theory are examples.) The weak and the strong interactions are neither universal nor geometric, so no. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? Because virtual particles are not matter. They are among the worst misunderstood things in popular accounts describing particle physics. Virtual particles arise in quantum field theory. An interaction in quantum field theory can be described by a nasty integral. Most of the time, that integral cannot be evaluated directly, but it can be evaluated by turning it into a power series: a some of ever smaller terms. Formally, these terms actually describe ever more complicated pathways of interaction between the two fields, but we can think of them as virtual particles. So instead of saying that we, say, accounted for how the field of electrons interacted with the electromagnetic field directly, and then through a secondary interaction with the electron field, etc., we now say that the “electron emitted a photon, and the split into a virtual electron-positron pair that then recombined into a final photon”. That “virtual electron-positron pair” is not something that existed, other than as a mental aid, a bookkeeping device, in the physicist’s mind. It is called “ virtual” because it does not exist. In contrast, the things described by Dirac’s equation are supposed to exist. They are not fancy bookkeeping devices. Question is, what are they? What do these solutions mean? Dirac originally thought that the oppositely charged solution might be the proton, but that didn’t work very well, since the proton does not have the same mass as the electron. Then came the “Dirac sea” business, the idea that the vacuum represents all negative energy states “filled in”, unless a particle is missing, and it’s this “hole” that Dirac’s equation describes. Sounds appealing, except that in the meantime, someone had the audacity to actually discover the positron, which fit nicely in Dirac’s equation! In the end, much of the paradoxical aspects of the Dirac equation vanish when we move on to quantum field theory. This is generally true: the quantum mechanics of particles works and it is useful, but it is obviously not a complete theory as it cannot account for particle creation and annihilation (which we observe) and violates causality (nonzero probabilities associated with faster-than-light and backward-in-time interactions). All this disappears with quantum field theory, which also offers a more natural home, so to speak, for antiparticles. Bottom line though, the negative energy solutions of the Dirac equation were associated with antiparticles because in the meantime, antiparticles (positrons) were actually discovered in experiment, and behaved just like Dirac’s equation described them. Isn't a supernova an instantaneous event? Why is it said that the last supernova was visible in the sky for 23 days? Shouldn't the explosion only be seen for some seconds? Have you seen motion pictures of large explosions? Nuclear tests? The actual explosion is as instantaneous as they come: it’s over in milliseconds or less. Yet in the first millisecond, you don’t even see much. It takes several seconds, minutes even, for the gigantic fireball to flare up, grow, reach its maximum brightness and eventually fade. And that’s a man-made explosion. Large by the standards of us lowly humans, but absolutely nothing compared to a supernova. An explosion that involves several times the mass of the Sun (i.e., several million times the mass of the Earth). An explosion that heats up this material to astonishing temperatures, causing it to fly apart in a gigantic fireball. So don’t be surprised if the light curve reaches its maximum only hours, or more likely, days after the actual event (depending on the type and size of the supernova); and especially don’t be surprised that it then takes weeks or months for the remnant to fade, as the fireball grows in size and becomes fainter. And of course it never quite goes away: e.g., here are the remnants of a fireball that was observed by Chinese astronomers 970 years ago, in 1054: It’s the famous Crab Nebula. In Newtonian gravity, what is the difference between the Poisson equation Δ(Φ) and the expression Φ=−GM/r for the gravitational potential Φ? Are both somewhat related? Oh, indeed they are profoundly related. Let’s start with Poisson’s equation, which presents a general relationship between the gravitational potential ϕ and the mass density ρ , both functions of the location r in space: ∇ 2 ϕ ( r ) = 4 π G ρ ( r ) . (1) How do you solve this equation? Without going into great detail, which can be found in relevant textbooks, the generic solution is obtained in the form of a Green’s function: ϕ ( r ) = − ∫ d 3 r ′ G ρ ( r ′ ) | r − r ′ | . Now let us assume that matter is in the form of a single mass point of mass M at some position r 0 . This can be represented using a three-dimensional Dirac delta-function: ρ = M δ 3 ( r − r 0 ) . When we substitute this into the Green’s function solution of Poisson’s equation, we get (as follows from the properties of the Dirac delta-function): ϕ ( r ) = − G M | r − r 0 | . Or, after denoting r = | r − r 0 | , ϕ ( r ) = − G M r . (2) In other words (2) is the solution of (1) in the specific case when the source of gravitation is a single point mass. Is the range of gravitational force infinite, diminishing toward but never reaching zero? None of the fundamental (or even not-so-fundamental) forces disappear, but the manner in which they diminish differs. Gravitation and electromagnetism are said to have “infinite” range, because the potential decreases “only” as the inverse of distance, and consequently, the force, which is to say, the gradient (rate of steepest change) diminishes as the inverse square of distance. So it still becomes rather tiny at a great distance from the source, but it’s still there. In contrast, forces mediated by massive particles in the quantum picture are said to have a “finite” range. Near the source, these forces behave just like gravity or electromagnetism. But when you reach a characteristic distance (which is proportional to the inverse of the mass of the force carrier particle) the potential, hence the force, begins to drop very rapidly, exponentially as a matter of fact. Examples fot this include the “weak” force (not really that weak, but it has a very finite range as the force carrier particles, the W and Z-bosons, are very massive), and also the “residual strong force”, aka. the “nuclear force” that is responsible for holding protons and neutrons together inside atoms. As to what the nuclear force is a residual of, whoa, things get really interesting there! The strong force, which holds quarks together, actually increases with distance! When the quarks are very close together, there’s barely any force. The quarks behave like free particles, or almost (this is called asymptotic freedom). But start pulling them apart and the force stiffens. You might think that this implies infinite range, but it really doesn’t; rather, when you pump enough energy into the system pulling two quarks apart, that energy is converted into a new quark-antiquark pair, and the bond “snaps”. Kind of like pulling a string: as you pull, eventually the string breaks, and you end up with two strings, with new endpoints. Ultimately of course all these pretty pictorial representations are just approximations; what we are really describing is a multitude of interacting quantum fields and their excited states. The “virtual particles” that may be used to describe them have no physical reality whatsoever; rather, they are convenient mathematical bookkeeping devices as we keep track of terms in a mathematical expression (a perturbative expansion). For a long-duration moon mission, would an Earth-corrected time standard be required, or would periodic corrections to Earth time be sufficient? It depends on what you want to achieve. As others noted, gravitational time dilation amounts to a roughly 60 microsecond difference per day. If you are only interested in making sure that you don’t miss your favorite TV show, you have nothing to worry about for at least a good half century, which is when the cumulative difference reaches about a second. But as they say, the devil is in the details[1]. What are you using your clocks for? If you are doing navigation using precise radio signals, GPS-like, then keep in mind that every microsecond amounts to about 300 meters when it comes to straightforward length measurements; depending on the geometry of the problem, when you are looking at satellites at an angle, the navigational errors can quickly add up to several kilometers. Needless to say, when you’re landing a spacecraft, several kilometers might mean the difference between a nice, flat region vs. the boulder-filled interior of a nasty lunar crater. Not good! Moreover, while it is true that the time dilation averages to about 60 microseconds a day, it is highly variable. The rate at which clocks tick on the Moon relative to terrestrial clocks (or clocks in intermediate orbits around the Earth, like GPS clocks) depends on many factors other than lunar gravity, including the gravity of the Earth itself, the gravitational field of the Sun (the Moon may be closer to, or farther from the Sun than the Earth at various points during a lunar orbit, and this affects relative clock rates) not to mention the relative motion of the respective clocks. Ultimately it is still a simple problem (just account for all the sources of gravitational time dilation and add them all up — nonlinear effects can likely be safely ignored as they are many orders of magnitude smaller) but it still requires making sure that everything is properly accounted for at the requisite level of accuracy. Long story short, my expectation is that before long, there will be a lunar reference time standard, likely as a result of some international agreement. Future missions, including missions that might be used to assist navigation in cislunar space, will probably use that standard. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

According to relativity, gravity slows time (time dilation) and causes length contraction? Does Dark Energy, which is accelerating the expansion of the Universe, speed time and cause lengthening is space? OK, it doesn't exactly work that way. Gravity doesn't slow time, speed time, or change lengths. However, according to the theory of RELATIVITY (never forget the name!) observers in different gravitational fields will measure things differently. So what takes 1 second according to the clock of an observer in a strong gravitational field may take 2 seconds according to the clock of an observer in a weak gravitational field. This of course implies that we have a spatially varying gravitational field, which changes from point to point. Cosmological models are usually homogeneous models: that is, they assume that on average, the gravitational field is the same everywhere, it only changes with time. Over time it becomes weaker in an expanding cosmos, because matter flies apart and becomes less dense. When dark energy is present, stuff flies apart faster. And the rate at which it flies apart decreases more slowly. The Hubble parameter, rather than going down to zero as matter becomes less and less dense, settles down on a nonzero value instead. Expansion continues. As a result of that expansion, there is redshift. Some of it is just plain old velocity-related Doppler, due to things flying apart. But some of it (over cosmological scales, especially) is due to the time-varying gravitational field. On average, matter is less dense today than yesterday, so its overall gravity is weaker today than yesterday, so clocks today appear to tick faster than clocks yesterday. A signal emitted billions of years ago at a certain number of oscillations per second will show fewer oscillations per second as measured by a clock today. Dark energy does not fundamentally change this, but it alters the rate at which cosmological parameters, including the redshift, evolve over time. Does the proton have a finite lifetime? What is the evidence for that? Please respond. This question is very important to me. I want your answer? There is no observational evidence of proton decay. The only evidence that we have is that if protons do decay, their half-life is incredibly long, on the order of 10 34 years or more. In the Standard Model of particle physics, there’s no mechanism for proton decay. As a general rule a decay happens if there exists a combination of particles with less rest mass-energy than the original particle, while preserving all strictly conserved quantities such as angular momentum or electric charge. There is no known “end product” for protons that would satisfy this criteria. You might wonder if perhaps an electrically neutral, zero-spin hydrogen atom might decay into something, but the answer again is no: combining an electron and a proton yields a neutron, which has more rest mass-energy than the hydrogen atom itself. Having said that, there is a possible decay route even for protons, or rather, I should say bulk matter, but on time scales much, much longer than a mere 10 34 years: quantum tunneling through a microscopic black hole state that instantaneously evaporates in the form of Hawking thermal radiation. Does such tunneling happen? I’d be inclined to say yes, but we’ll likely never know, as it is not going to be observable by any conceivable experiment. If excitations in the "electron field” look to us like electrons and positrons, and excitations in the "photon field” look to us like photons, what do we perceive excitations in the "electric field" or "magnetic field" or "gravitational field" as? Electric and magnetic fields are both manifestations of the electromagnetic field (i.e., the “photon field”). How the electromagnetic field appears to split into these components is observer-dependent. For instance, an observer standing next to an electron will see an electrostatic field and no magnetic field; another, moving observer, looking at the same charge, would see a time-varying electric field in his moving reference frame, along with a magnetic field. Whether or not the gravitational field is a quantum field remains an open question. However, given how weak the gravitational interaction is, we may never be able to “perceive” gravitons directly with any conceivable present or future experiment.
