What is the significance of the constant "c" in Maxwell's equations? Why does light travel at such a high speed? Whether a speed is high or low is in the eye of the beholder. Many who dream of interstellar travel think that the speed of light is way too low. But the significance? Maxwell’s equations describe the interplay between electric and magnetic fields, the former being sourced by charges and currents. There is a specific subclass of solutions to these equations in the absence of charges and currents: vacuum solutions, which turn out to be propagating plane waves. The speed of propagation corresponds to the observed electric and magnetic properties of the vacuum. Although these properties are not really properties of the vacuum per se; if we go beyond Maxwell, to quantum electrodynamics, we find that these properties are ultimately related to the “fine structure constant” (never mind the name, it has historic origins) that characterizes the strength of the electromagnetic interaction. Relativity theory is originally based on the idea that the nature of the electromagnetic interaction is the same for all observers, regardless of their motion relative to each other. This means that the speed that is derived for the electromagnetic field in the vacuum is itself an invariant speed, in fact, the invariant speed, of the theory. We can now turn the tables around and make this existence of an invariant speed a fundamental principle; we then find that any theory like Maxwell’s, which involves a “massless field”, will yield vacuum solutions that propagate at this invariant speed of relativity theory. Is this speed large? Or small? Well… how about if I told you that it is exactly 1? That is to say, anything moving at the vacuum speed of light moves exactly one “natural unit of distance” over one “natural unit of time”. So maybe the right question to ask is not why the vacuum speed of light is so high, but why the speeds in our everyday experience are so low. Why do we live in the nonrelativistic limit? I mean, imagine if we were made of stuff that exists in the deep interior of hot stars: a relativistic plasma. Particles, atomic nuclei, electrons, would all move around at relativistic speeds! The trouble is, when everything has that much kinetic energy, almost nothing sticks together. Things bounce around but do not form complex structures. If we want complex structures, we need to cool things down. Way, way down. The energies of chemical reactions are many orders below relativistic energies. When we cool things down this much, suddenly we have complexity. Chemical bonds. Complex molecules. Life. Think about it for a moment. If you were transported to the interior of a star, you would not know it. Before any sensation could reach your brain, your entire body would cease to exist, effectively instantaneously. Contrast this with being transported into deep space, far from any heat or light source. It would not be a pleasant experience to be sure, but you would stay alive, even conscious and able to function, for several seconds! Your physical body is far, far more compatible with the emptiness of space than with the high temperature environment of a star (need not even be relativistic temperatures). So there. It’s not the speed of light that is fast. It is us, nonrelativistic creatures, living on the edge of empty space and absolute zero, who are slow. Really, really, really slow. The upside of it (yes, there is an upside) is that we probably live a lot longer as a result. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

How is the speed of gravity determined? First of all, while I recognize that this is a bit of semantics, there is no “speed of gravity” any more than there is a “speed of electromagnetism”. Gravity is an interaction, it does not have an inherent speed. However, influences in the gravitational field, far from sources, travel as transverse waves, and these indeed do have a speed. Theory tells us that this speed is the same as the speed of influences in the electromagnetic field, i.e., electromagnetic waves such as light. While few had real doubts that this prediction is valid, its first observational test came seven years ago with the LIGO event GW170817. This gravitational wave event turned out to be the collision and merger of a pair of neutron stars, an event that was also detectable in a multitude of electromagnetic frequencies. The electromagnetic and gravitational signals arrived at the same time, even though they event took place some 130 million light years from here. This tells us that indeed, gravitational and electromagnetic waves traveled at the same speed. As a matter of fact, this had a direct impact on theory. There are proposed alternative theories of gravitation in which there is not one but two (or more) metrical fields, one determining the speed of gravitational waves, the other, the speed of electromagnetic waves. These “bimetric” theories were essentially falsified by the GW170817 observation.

If we accept that dark matter exist, they must be part of the entire planet Earth, including living plant and animal organisms. In this case, is it correct to believe that dark matter is part of the human organism? If dark matter exists, it is indeed presumed to be present everywhere, though its density is very low compared to terrestrial densities. However, I’d hesitate to call it a “part of”, e.g., organisms. By way of an example that is known to exist with certainty, right now there are countless neutrinos going through your body. Are they part of your body? Not really. Why? Because neutrinos are effectively non-interacting. To them, your body might as well not be there. And vice versa, for your body the presence of the neutrinos makes no difference. Neutrinos still interact with ordinary matter though, just very, very, very weakly. An awful lot of neutrinos would be needed to make a noticeable difference. Sure, if you happened to be situated near an exploding supernova, the neutrino flux might be enough to evaporate you in an instant, but for that, the explosion of an entire giant star would be required, fairly close to you. In contrast, the millions, billions, trillions of neutrinos that pass through your body right this moment make no difference whatsoever. They are not part of you. The presumed dark matter of cosmology interacts even less with ordinary matter. So even if it is present right here, right now, it is not part of you, of animals, plants, or the Earth. It happens to be in the same place in space at the same time, but it might as well be in another galaxy far, far away: There is no interaction, no connection between that dark matter medium and your body. Since the Bekenstein Bound and BH event horizons are the most information dense places possible, how probable is it that they are conscious? I think this question was inspired, in part, by a misconception of the meaning, “information”. Allow me to show two character sequences of approximately equal length. First, this: To be, or not to be: that is the question: Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, Or to take arms against a sea of troubles. And now this: 8RfUd8yHHftN5juY5MPME1SxwcE7lNOAjjo6Q1jlKyK0hdwk 8DU86TeOGcyJZ1Gk2cEMAtRlBK1G0Sy1WU2xFwJ4sBCeQv15 qBV4pJKGcY28npr4GBDXoJQ1aHw09P9xGrJMqjJ3Jj8pXRWO C5jUXwiEWn2cLNFH91Qxnws3 Which of these contain more “information”? It is understandable if you thought it was the first example. The second case is, after all, just some printable ASCII gibberish, no useful content whatsoever. But that does not mean no information! In fact, if you feed both examples to compression algorithms, you will find that the algorithm does a much better job compressing Shakespeare’s lines than the random sequence of letters. In the end, significantly fewer bytes, significantly less information is needed to fully reconstruct the first example compared to the second. But we don’t even need abstract algorithms. Let me show you what I mean: To b, or nt to b: tht s th qstn: Whethr 'ts noblr in th mnd to suffr Th slngs nd arrws of outrgs frtne, Or to tk arms gnst a sea of trbls. Look at this text. I am betting that if you are a native English speaker, you have no trouble reading it even though almost 20% of the letters are missing. You can still unambiguously reconstruct the original. In contrast, if I were to remove but a single letter from the second example containing gibberish, you’d have no way of knowing what that letter was. There is no redundancy. Everything there is important information. We tend to associate information with order. We think there is more information in, say, in a picture on the CRT of an old-fashioned analog television set as opposed to the “snow” we see when the channel is not broadcasting. But in reality, the opposite is true: random noise carries a lot more information than an orderly broadcast. Of course no one said that that information is of any use. Put enough monkeys behind typewriters and the result may even include the four lines of Shakespeare above. But it will also include all other possible combinations of 170-odd letters and symbols, and you’d have no way of knowing what is useful and what is not. So no, a black hole’s event horizon is not conscious. If anything, it’s the opposite. Imagine your brain scrambled in a food processor. The result represents a lot more “information”! If we ever discover something that defied the laws of physics, would we be adding a new topic in physics or questioning whether or not our laws and ideas in physics were all wrong? Throughout the history of modern science, progress was made when we discovered something that defined the laws of physics known at the time. These challenges were met by making sense of what we saw, and ultimately, revising and improving our understanding of Nature. The “laws of physics” are not dogma, not some unchanging commandments from the deities of the physical sciences or anything like that. They simply reflect our present understanding of how Nature works. Challenges are welcome, especially when they are unexpected, as it is thanks to those challenges that progress is made. No, progress does not mean questioning whether our ideas “were all wrong”. We know that they are not all wrong: our ideas have been well tested through observation and experiment and they have a very good track record, successfully predicting results. So they cannot be “all wrong”. That does not mean that they are the final word on any particular topic. Take classical mechanics, for instance. It all seemed so nice and simple, back in the 18th century. But then, those pesky engineers invented steam engines. Engines producing mechanical energy out of… what exactly? Heat? What is heat? How is it related to motion? It took decades before physicists began to make sense of all this, after exploring some remarkable detours, eventually discarding concepts like caloricum and finally arriving at modern formulations of axiomatic thermodynamics and statistical physics. Or how about the luminiferous ether theory, which made perfect sense in light of Maxwell’s equations… that is, until it didn’t, in light of the famous (and, by the standards of the day, very surprising) Michelson-Morley null result, eventually leading to relativity theory? Or how about Rutherford’s surprising result? Bombard a thin gold foil with alpha particles. They should pass through with minimal deflection, according to the then-popular model of the atom, Thomson’s. But they didn’t. Some of the alpha particles were actually reflected! To quote Rutherford, “It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.” And sure, it led to a major revision of our understanding of atoms, another step in the early 20th century towards modern particle physics. So you see, surprising discoveries happen all the time. We love them! They let us learn something new. As to how we respond to them, it depends on the nature of the discovery. Sometimes, it opens a whole new chapter in physics (e.g., thermodynamics, relativity theory, quantum theory). Sometimes it leads to a refinement or improved understanding within an existing framework (e.g., Rutherford’s atomic model). In all cases, it means we can take another meaningful step forward. Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time? Oh, in quantum mechanics, a particle like an electron is always a particle, an actual, immutable particle. The waves (which is to say, the wavefunction) determine the physical properties, including the position and momentum of this particle. In the Copenhagen interpretation, this wavefunction is interpreted as a probability amplitude, and it is used in conjunction with the concept of an idealized, classical measurement apparatus, to compute the probability of finding the electron somewhere, or moving with some momentum. In quantum field theory, there are no particles, only fields. The fields are quantum fields, which is to say, just like the position of that poor electron in quantum mechanics, the field does not have definite values at specific places and times; rather, a wavefunction determines (at least in the Copenhagen interpretation) the probability of finding the field with specific values at specific places and times. However, another property of these quantum fields is that when they interact, their values go up or down one unit at a time. It is these unit excitations that we observe, in localized interactions, with particle-like behavior. So to sum up/reiterate, in quantum field theory, an electron is an excitation of the corresponding fermionic field (the electron field). The wavefunction (not to be confused with the field proper) may be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probabilities of finding the field in a definite state using a classical instrument. Interactions between fields create and destroy excitations (“particles”). In contrast, in quantum mechanics particles are eternal, there are no fields, and the wavefunction can be interpreted as a probability amplitude that tells us the probability of finding the particle in some state somewhere using a classical instrument. A system composed by a piece of iron and a magnet has more energy if the iron is closer the magnet. So, the overall weight should be (very very slightly) different. Is there an intuitive thought experiment to show it? Actually, when you bring a piece of iron to a magnet, the system has less energy when the iron is closer to the magnet. You need to invest energy, do work to separate the iron from the magnet. The amount of energy is usually minuscule so it is not something we can measure, but to offer an intuition: Suppose you have a magnet and you release a piece of iron nearby. The magnet attracts it: the piece of iron accelerates, gaining kinetic energy at the expense of losing potential energy. The overall energy-content of the system remains the same. Then finally, the piece of iron hits the magnet and stops moving. Its kinetic energy now transforms into the random motion of its and the magnet’s molecules, i.e., it gets converted into heat. That heat is then radiated away into the environment as both the piece of iron and the magnet cool down th ambient temperature. The amount of energy lost by way of that waste heat radiated away is precisely the amount by which the mass-energy of the system decreases. Of course as I said, the amount is minuscule. Far, far less than what we could possibly measure even with our most sensitive instruments. However, similar processes that go on either on the nuclear scale (much large energies) or simply on a much larger mass scale (e.g., astrophysical systems) do have measurable properties that explicitly confirm this description. Going back to the piece of iron and the magnet, to remove the piece of iron the process needs to be reversed. A force must be applied to separate the piece of iron from the magnet and move it some distance away. The work done by this force is now the potential energy of the system, i.e., its ability to make the piece of iron move again if it were to be released, allowed again to accelerate towards the magnet. Is there observational evidence confirming the slowdown phase of the universe billions of years ago, or are these only theoretical conclusions? It is somewhat unclear* what this question is about, as I can think of at least two cases of “slowdown” in modern cosmology. First, the end of inflation. In the inflationary model, the very early cosmos underwent a period of exponential expansion. This speculative idea is supposed to solve several issues with cosmology, including the “flatness problem”, i.e., why the universe is so uniform even today: Characterized by no or negligible spatial curvature and a uniform average mass density. If the “visible universe” really represents just a tiny, tiny part of the pre-inflationary universe, the problem would be solved. Or not… none other than one of the “founding fathers” of inflationary cosmology, Paul Steinhardt, expressed serious concerns that while inflation solves some problems, the price we pay is that it introduces problems more severe than the ones it addresses. In any case, we have no direct evidence of inflation or how it may have come to an end. It is, at present, an entirely theoretical and speculative idea. Second, perhaps the question referred to the “dark ages”, the period of time between the moment when the universe beame transparent (the so-called surface of last scattering, when the cosmic microwave background radiation was born) and the moment when the first stars began to appear (reionization). The problem is that some of the structures that emerged in the early universe are much too large and emerged much too quickly to make sense. So what if, in fact, during these “dark ages” the expansion of the universe experienced a slowdown, so the universe is actually older than we think it is, with more time available for early large structures to form? Makes a lot of sense, but this, too, is a highly speculative concept with no observational support. It is hard to study the early history of the cosmos. We do not see “behind” the cosmic microwave background and we also have no direct observational evidence of the “dark ages”, as there were no sources of light during this time. *I’ve since been enlightened that the question was originally intended to be about the first 9 billion years, give or take, of the history of the universe during which the rate of expansion was slowing down, as opposed to the last roughly 5 billion years when it began accelerating due to dark energy. This is pretty much based on direct evidence, in particular the Type Ia supernova data that led to discovery of accelerating expansion and earned its discoverers a Nobel-prize in 2011. Can Schrodinger's equation be proven to accurately describe quantum mechanics? Are there alternative methods for dealing with quantum mechanics? Schrödinger’s equation defines nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. It can be deduced from the classical Hamiltonian, or from the canonical commutation relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , but either way: nonrelativistic quantum mechanics is Schrödinger’s equation. It’s not “proven” (never will be) beyond showing that the math is self-consistent; is is validated when experiments confirm the equation’s predictions. There are, of course, alternatives. There is relativistic quantum particle mechanics in the form of Dirac’s equation. There is relativistic quantum field theory, which kind of implies either the Dirac or the Schrödinger equation in the appropriate limit. And then there are tentative theoretical approaches that attempt to generalize the commutation relation, e.g., by introducing a length scale. The Dirac equation and quantum field theory (in the form of the Standard Model of particle physics) are mathematically self-consistent and are validated by experiment. Alternatives, not so much. Even when the math itself is robust, there is no validation in the form of observational evidence. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is there a semantic difference between the redshift caused by gravity wells and the redshift caused by the expansion of space? First of all, allow me to take exception at the (granted, commonly used) expression, “expansion of space”. Space is not a thing. More specifically, it does not have any little markers attached to it by which its expansion, if any, could even be measured! No, it is things (galaxies, gas, dust, etc.) that are flying apart. It is the density of matter that decreases over time. And it is the gravitational field that changes as a result: a physical field that, however, can also be interpreted as the metric of spacetime. It is when folks take this interpretation a little too literally and a little too dogmatically that we end up with “expansion of space”. So then, putting these qualms aside… redshift happens as a result of the relationship between the world lines of the transmitter and the receiver. If the distance (the actual distance, which may be measurable by means of exchanging light signals, for instance) between the transmitter and the receiver changes over time, there is a velocity-induced Doppler frequency shift. If clocks at the different locations (or times!) tick at different rates, there is a gravity-induced redshift (gravity manifests itself primarily in the form of time dilation in general relativity, i.e., the rates at which clocks tick relative to one another.) It is time dilation that yields an observed redshift for light coming from a gravitational well, and it is predominantly time dilation when it comes to the redshift of “high-z” objects, that is, objects very far from here with substantial redshifts. There are some qualitative differences: when it comes to a gravitational well, we’re basically looking at a static configuration, and simply the fact that clocks deep inside that gravitational well tick slower, right now, than clocks elsewhere. When it comes to cosmological redshift, what we see is that in the distant past, matter was much denser, consequently the average gravitational potential was greater and clocks were ticking more slowly back then than they tick today. So truly, it’s gravitational redshift in both cases, just two distinct scenarios: One is the gravitational redshift due to a compact object’s gravitational field here and now, the other is gravitational redshift due to the average gravitational field characterizing the cosmos in the distant past. But fundamentally, it’s gravity in both cases. A consequence of Einstein’s field equations that connect, no, not the “geometry of spacetime” but rather, the tensor field of gravitation with the stress-energy-momentum of matter. It’s due to the weak equivalence principle that we can interpret the tensor field of gravitation as geometry, but as I stressed in many of my answers in the past, Einstein himself cautioned against taking this interpretation too literally. Otherwise it becomes an obstacle, preventing us from thinking about alternate theories of gravity that may not obey the weak equivalence principle, or quantizing gravity as a force.
